title: French Indochina & British Malaya
titleline: French Indochina & British Malaya - The History Web
para1: French Indochina and British Malaya. Mainland Southeast Asia between Siam and the South China Sea was divided in the nineteenth century between two empires. France built French Indochina: beginning with the conquest of southern Vietnam (Cochinchina, 1862) and a protectorate over Cambodia (1863), it consolidated Vietnam, Cambodia, and later Laos (1899) into a single Indochinese Union in 1887, ruled from Saigon and then, after 1902, from Hanoi. France drained the colony's resources - rice, rubber, and opium - while its schools and hospitals served mostly the French and a small native elite.
para2: Britain built British Malaya: from its base at Penang (1786), it assembled the Straits Settlements - Penang, Malacca, and Singapore - as direct Crown colonies after a period of East India Company control, and extended protectorates over the Malay sultanates. British Malaya became one of the empire's most profitable possessions, the world's largest producer of tin and later rubber, with George Town and Singapore as great entrepot ports.
para3: Both empires squeezed their colonies for revenue. In Indochina Governor-General Paul Doumer reorganized the administration at the turn of the century and pushed roads, bridges and the great railway from Saigon to Hanoi, paid for by state monopolies on salt, alcohol and opium and by heavy taxes that provoked peasant risings. In Malaya, British Residents ruled through the sultans while Chinese and Indian immigrants poured in to work the tin mines and, after 1900, the rubber estates that soon made Malaya the world's chief rubber producer. The schools and offices of both colonies created small Western-educated native elites - and it was from those elites that the first nationalist movements came.
para4: Resistance to both empires began early. In Vietnam the scholars of the Can Vuong movement fought France into the 1890s, and in the new century the mandarin Phan Boi Chau sent young men to study in Japan and wrote stirring appeals for Vietnam's liberation. In Malaya, Malay teachers and religious reformers and the Straits Chinese merchants of Penang and Singapore began to organize associations of their own. By the early 1920s both colonies stood at the height of their prosperity - and beneath the surface the colonial order was already being questioned by a generation its own schools had trained.

title: Ottoman Syria and Mesopotamia
titleline: Ottoman Syria and Mesopotamia - The History Web
para1: Ottoman Syria and Mesopotamia. For four centuries, from 1516 to 1918, the Arab lands of Syria and Mesopotamia were provinces of the Ottoman Empire - an era that shaped their cities, their sectarian geography, and ultimately their modern borders. The era began with Sultan Selim I's lightning campaign of 1516-1517: victory over the Mamluks at Marj Dabiq near Aleppo gave him Syria; the following year Egypt itself fell, and the Arab heartlands passed from Cairo to Constantinople.
para2: Ottoman Syria - the whole country between the Taurus mountains and Sinai - was governed from Damascus, then divided into the eyalets of Aleppo, Tripoli, and Sidon; Mount Lebanon won special autonomous status as early as 1667. The 19th century brought both reform and tragedy: the Tanzimat decrees of 1839 and 1856 declared Muslims and non-Muslims equal, but the old hierarchy's collapse fed sectarian violence - massacres of Christians at Aleppo in 1850 and, worst of all, in Damascus and Mount Lebanon in 1860. European pressure then forced the creation of the Mount Lebanon Mutasarrifate in 1861, an autonomous Christian-governed province - the seed of modern Lebanon. By the 1870s the region was organized into the vilayets of Syria, Aleppo, and Beirut, with Jerusalem an autonomous mutasarrifate.
para3: Mesopotamia followed its own rhythm. Suleiman the Magnificent conquered Baghdad from the Safavids in 1534, and for three centuries Iraq was the contested frontier of the Ottoman-Persian wars - Baghdad even fell to the Safavids from 1623 to 1638 before the Ottomans recovered it. From 1749 to 1831 the region was governed by a semi-autonomous dynasty of Georgian Mamluks ruling in the sultan's name; after their removal, the reforming governor Midhat Pasha modernized the provinces of Mosul, Baghdad, and Basra.
para4: The First World War ended Ottoman rule in both lands: British forces took Baghdad in 1917 and swept through Palestine and Syria in 1918. The empire's Arab provinces became British and French mandates - Iraq, Palestine, Syria, and Lebanon - and the borders drawn in those years are the borders on the map today.

title: The Afsharid & Zand Dynasties
titleline: The Afsharid & Zand Dynasties - The History Web
para1: The Afsharid and Zand Dynasties. Between the fall of the Safavids and the rise of the Qajars, 18th-century Iran passed through two short, vivid dynasties: the Afsharid empire of the conqueror Nader Shah (1736-1796) and the gentler Zand dynasty (1751-1794) of Karim Khan. Together they form the violent, brilliant interlude of modern Iranian history.
para2: Nader Shah was one of the most astonishing soldiers of the age: born into a poor semi-nomadic family of the Afshar tribe in Khorasan, he rose from local warlord to expel the Afghan invaders, recover Iran's lost provinces from the Ottomans and Russians, and in 1736 crown himself Shah. Under him Iran reached its greatest extent since the ancient Sasanians - from the Caucasus to Central Asia. His most famous campaign was the invasion of Mughal India: at Karnal in 1739 he crushed a Mughal army six times the size of his own, took Delhi, and carried off the imperial treasury - some seven hundred million rupees, the Peacock Throne, and the Koh-i-Noor and Daria-i-Noor diamonds.
para3: But Nader's later years darkened into cruelty, and in 1747 he was assassinated by his own officers. His empire shattered at once: Ahmad Shah Abdali founded the Durrani Empire in Afghanistan, and an Afsharid rump clung on only in Khorasan until 1796. Into the vacuum stepped Karim Khan Zand, who from 1751 ruled most of Iran - not as Shah but under the modest title Vakil ol-Ra'aya, 'regent of the people.' His twenty-eight-year reign was a rare interval of stability between the era of Nader's conquests and the rise of the Qajars.
para4: Karim Khan's death in 1779 unleashed civil war among his heirs. The last Zand, the young and chivalrous Lotf Ali Khan, fought a doomed resistance against the rising Qajar chieftain Agha Mohammad Khan and was defeated and deposed in 1794. With him ended the age of Nader and Karim Khan - and began the century of the Qajars.

title: The Ayutthaya Kingdom
titleline: The Ayutthaya Kingdom - The History Web
para1: The Ayutthaya Kingdom. The Ayutthaya Kingdom (1351-1767) was the great kingdom of Siam, the forerunner of modern Thailand - and one of the richest and most cosmopolitan states in early modern Asia. Founded on an island in the Chao Phraya river in 1351, it began as a maritime confederation of city-states drawing tribute from the post-Srivijaya world, then centralized over two centuries into a powerful kingdom. European travellers in the early 1500s ranked Ayutthaya one of the three great powers of Asia, alongside Vijayanagara and Ming China.
para2: Ayutthaya fought its neighbors for centuries - above all Burma. It was a vassal of the Burmese Toungoo empire from 1569 to 1584 before regaining its independence, and in the following centuries its culture flourished. In the seventeenth century the city became a great centre of international trade: under King Narai (r. 1657-1688), Persian and then European influence was strong, and a Siamese embassy dazzled the court of Louis XIV in 1686. The kingdom's later years, built on booming Chinese trade, have been called a golden age of Siamese culture.
para3: The same period brought danger. Ayutthaya never settled a reliable order of succession, and its elite quarrels weakened the kingdom just as Burma's new Konbaung dynasty rose. Burmese armies invaded in 1759-1760 and again in 1765, and after a fourteen-month siege, on 7 April 1767, Ayutthaya fell. The city was destroyed so completely that the 417-year-old kingdom ended with it - its libraries, palaces, and temples burned.
para4: Siam recovered with remarkable speed: within fifteen years the Siamese had reunited under new capitals at Thonburi and then Bangkok. But Ayutthaya was never rebuilt, and its monumental ruins stand today as the kingdom's memorial - the remains of what was once one of the largest and most splendid cities in the world.

title: The British East India Company
titleline: The British East India Company - The History Web
para1: The British East India Company. The British East India Company (1600-1874) was the strangest empire in history: a private joint-stock company that conquered a subcontinent. Chartered by Queen Elizabeth I on the last day of 1600 with a monopoly on English trade east of the Cape of Good Hope, it began as a spice venture - but Dutch competition in the East Indies drove it to India, where a naval victory over the Portuguese at Swally in 1612 won it Mughal favor and its first mainland footholds.
para2: For a century and a half it was a trading company pure and simple - and a colossally successful one: by the mid-1700s it accounted for half of world trade in cotton, silk, indigo, saltpetre, tea, and later opium. Then it became a state. At Plassey in 1757 its army defeated the Nawab of Bengal, and province by province - by treaty, intrigue, and war - the Company swallowed the subcontinent. At its peak it was the largest corporation in the world, with three presidency armies totaling some 260,000 soldiers, at times twice the size of the British Army itself.
para3: Company rule was extraction: its taxes, wrung from the countryside by force, impoverished Bengal - where company policy helped turn drought into the Great Famine of 1770, in which an estimated ten million people starved - while its opium trade with China added another notorious stream of profit.
para4: The reckoning came in 1857: the great rebellion of the Company's own Indian soldiers shook its rule to its foundations. When the smoke cleared, Parliament ended the experiment: the Government of India Act 1858 transferred everything - armies, provinces, revenues - to the British Crown, and the British Raj began. The Company itself lingered as a trading shell until 1874, when it was dissolved. But its century of rule had already decided India's fate for the next two hundred years.

title: The British Raj
titleline: The British Raj - The History Web
para1: The British Raj began in 1858, when the British Crown took direct responsibility for government in India. It began after the great rebellion of 1857: by the Government of India Act of 1858, the East India Company's vast conquests passed to Queen Victoria, who in 1876 was proclaimed Empress of India. A viceroy governed from Calcutta - after 1911 from the new imperial capital at Delhi - ruling both the directly administered provinces of British India and, through 'paramountcy,' the hundreds of princely states whose maharajas kept their thrones under British suzerainty.
para2: The Raj was an empire of superlatives and contradictions. It unified the subcontinent under one administration, one army, and one railway network; it also drained India's wealth to Britain - as Indian nationalists charged - through unfair trade, restraint of Indian industry, and taxes paying British salaries. At its greatest extent it embraced nearly all of today's India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Myanmar, with Aden and the Persian Gulf states attached at various times.
para3: Indian nationalism grew up inside the Raj's own institutions: the Indian National Congress, founded in Bombay in 1885 by Western-educated professionals, moved from loyal petition to the demand for self-rule; the Muslim League followed in 1906; and after the First World War the freedom struggle became a mass movement that no viceroy could contain.
para4: The First World War changed everything. India's soldiers and taxpayers had sustained Britain's war effort, and the reward - the Montagu-Chelmsford reforms of 1919, offering a limited share of power in the provinces - fell far short of self-rule. The same year the Rowlatt Acts authorized detention without trial, and in April 1919 General Dyer's troops fired on an unarmed crowd in Amritsar's Jallianwala Bagh, killing hundreds, a massacre that shattered Indian faith in British justice. Mohandas Gandhi, newly returned from South Africa, answered with non-cooperation: from 1920 to 1922 millions boycotted British courts, schools, titles and cloth, until Gandhi suspended the campaign after a crowd killed policemen at Chauri Chaura. The Raj had reached its greatest extent - but the age of mass nationalism had begun.

title: The Dutch East Indies
titleline: The Dutch East Indies - The History Web
para1: The Dutch East Indies. The Dutch East Indies - the Netherlands' vast colony in the Indonesian archipelago - was the prize possession of the Dutch Empire and the ancestor of modern Indonesia. It began as the empire of a company: the Dutch East India Company (VOC) had seized the spice trade from the Portuguese in the 1600s and built its capital at Batavia (modern Jakarta). When the bankrupt VOC was dissolved, the Dutch state took its possessions over on the last day of 1799, and the colony proper was born in 1800. A French and British interregnum interrupted Dutch rule during the Napoleonic Wars, but the Netherlands regained the islands in 1816.
para2: The nineteenth century made it one of the most profitable colonies in the world. Dutch armies fought a long series of wars that brought the whole archipelago - Java, Sumatra, Borneo, Sulawesi, and finally western New Guinea - under one rule. The infamous Cultivation System forced Javanese peasants to grow export crops for the government; later, private plantations poured out coffee, sugar, tea, rubber, and oil for the world market, while Indonesian nationalism began to stir in response.
para3: The turn of the century brought a new conscience and a new policy: the Ethical Policy, proclaimed in 1901, promised irrigation, education and welfare for Indonesians, though its benefits proved limited and uneven. Indonesian nationalism grew up inside the colony's own new institutions: Budi Utomo, founded by Javanese students in 1908, was the first native association; Sarekat Islam, born as a league of batik traders, became by the late 1910s a mass movement claiming millions of members; and in 1914 Dutch and Indonesian radicals founded the Indies Social Democratic Association, forerunner of the archipelago's communist party.
para4: In 1918 the Dutch answered the new politics with the Volksraad, a largely advisory People's Council with limited Indonesian representation - reform enough to raise hopes, not enough to satisfy them. Strikes spread through the railways, docks and sugar estates in the early 1920s, and the colonial government met them with surveillance, exile and internment. The East Indies of 1924 was still among the most profitable colonies in the world, but the quiet order the Dutch prized had already been broken by an organized Indonesian national movement.

title: The Dzungar Khanate
titleline: The Dzungar Khanate - The History Web
para1: The Dzungar Khanate. The Dzungar Khanate (1634-1758) was the last great nomadic empire of the steppe - the state of the Oirat, the western Mongols, who from their homeland in Dzungaria (northern Xinjiang) built a realm stretching from southern Siberia to Tibet. Tibetan Buddhism was its faith, the horse its power, and for a century it stood as the Qing dynasty's most dangerous rival for the mastery of Inner Asia.
para2: The Oirats united in the Junggar Basin around 1620, and the khanate took shape under Erdeni Batur. Its greatest khans were conquerors: Galdan, who received the title Boshugtu Khan from the Dalai Lama in 1678, conquered the Tarim Basin and crushed the Khalkha Mongols before the Qing defeated him and stripped him of Outer Mongolia in 1696. His successor Tsewang Rabtan went further - in 1717 Dzungar cavalry seized Lhasa itself, holding Tibet until the Qing drove them out in 1720. Under Galdan Tseren (r. 1727-1745) the khanate's armies ranged as far west as Tashkent and the Fergana Valley.
para3: The end came from within. After Galdan Tseren's death the khanate tore itself apart in civil war - and the Qing emperor Qianlong saw his chance. Between 1755 and 1758 Qing armies conquered Dzungaria and, in a campaign of annihilation remembered as the Dzungar genocide, wiped out the Dzungar people - a whole nation erased from its homeland.
para4: The destruction of the Dzungars redrew the map of Asia: it opened the way to the Qing conquest of Mongolia and Tibet, and created 'Xinjiang' - the 'New Frontier' - as a province of China on the emptied land. The last nomadic empire of the steppe had fallen, and with it ended the age when horsemen could challenge empires.

title: The Joseon Dynasty (Korea)
titleline: The Joseon Dynasty (Korea) - The History Web
para1: The Joseon Dynasty (Korea). The Joseon dynasty (1392-1897) ruled Korea for 505 years - longer than any other royal house of its era - and made Korea in its own image. It was founded by the general Yi Seong-gye, who overthrew the Goryeo kingdom in 1392, took the throne as King Taejo, and moved the capital to Hanseong, modern Seoul. Under his heirs the kingdom pushed its borders north to the Amnok (Yalu) and Tuman rivers - essentially Korea's borders today.
para2: Joseon remade Korea on Neo-Confucian principles: Buddhism was pushed aside and its followers at times persecuted, and a scholar-official elite (the yangban) governed through civil service examinations. The dynasty's greatest king, Sejong the Great (r. 1418-1450), presided over a golden age of science and culture - and gave Korea its greatest treasure: hangul, the Korean alphabet, promulgated in 1446 so that ordinary people could read and write.
para3: The kingdom survived its trials. Japan's warlord Toyotomi Hideyoshi invaded in 1592 and 1597, devastating the peninsula, but Admiral Yi Sun-sin's navy - with its armored 'turtle ships' - cut Japanese supply lines and saved the kingdom. Manchu invasions in 1627 and 1636-37 forced Joseon to accept Qing overlordship, after which Korea turned inward for nearly two centuries of peace as the 'hermit kingdom.'
para4: The end came in the age of empire: pressed by Japan, Russia, and the Western powers, King Gojong proclaimed the Korean Empire in 1897, but Japan annexed Korea outright in 1910, ending five centuries of the dynasty. Joseon's legacy - hangul, Confucian institutions, and the Korean nation itself - endured through thirty-five years of Japanese rule and into the two Koreas of today.

title: The Kazakh Khanate
titleline: The Kazakh Khanate - The History Web
para1: The Kazakh Khanate. The Kazakh Khanate (1465-1847) was the last great nomadic state of the Eurasian steppe - the empire of the Kazakh people, heirs of the Golden Horde, who ruled the vast grasslands of what is now Kazakhstan for nearly four centuries. It was founded around 1465 by Kerei and Janibek, two princes who broke away from the fragmenting Uzbek Khanate to carve out their own realm on the steppe - the first nation-state in Central Asia created by a modern ethnic group itself.
para2: The khanate was a true nomadic empire: its power was the horse, the felt yurt, and the great tribal confederations. Over the 17th century the Kazakhs organized themselves into three hordes or zhuz - the Senior, the Middle, and the Junior - each with its own territory and seasonal migrations. After the death of Tauke Khan in the early 18th century, the zhuz became effectively independent khanates, and the unity of the steppe was lost.
para3: The brief restoration came under Ablai Khan, who reunified the Kazakhs and skillfully balanced the two empires closing in on the steppe - Russia from the north and Qing China from the east. After his death in 1781 the khanate fractured again, and this time the Russian advance could not be stopped: in 1822-1824 the Tsar's government abolished the khanate institution itself by statute, placing the steppe under direct imperial administration.
para4: The Kazakhs answered with their last national rising: Kenesary Qasymuly proclaimed himself khan in 1837 and fought Russian rule for ten years until his death in 1847. With him ended four centuries of steppe empire - the last chapter of the world the Mongols had made. The steppe passed under the Tsars, and the Kazakhs began the long road that would lead, a century and a half later, to an independent Kazakhstan.

title: The Konbaung Kingdom
titleline: The Konbaung Kingdom - The History Web
para1: The Konbaung Kingdom. The Konbaung dynasty (1752-1885) was the last royal house of Burma - the 'Third Burmese Empire' - and its story is the story of a proud kingdom ground down by the British Empire. It was founded in 1752 by Alaungpaya, a village headman from Shwebo who rose against the Mon conquerors of the fallen Toungoo dynasty, reunified Burma by 1757, and built the second-largest empire in Burmese history, ruling at its height some three million subjects under a royal anthem that proclaimed 'The Whole Southern Island Belongs To Him.'
para2: Under Alaungpaya's heirs - above all the long-reigning Bodawpaya (1782-1819) - Konbaung Burma expanded in every direction, conquering Arakan, invading Siam (and destroying Ayutthaya in 1767), and pressing into Manipur and Assam. The dynasty continued the administrative reforms of its predecessors and laid the foundations of the modern Burmese state, shifting its capital between Ava, Amarapura, and finally the new royal city of Mandalay, founded in 1857.
para3: Expansion brought collision with British India. Three Anglo-Burmese Wars decided Burma's fate: the first (1824-1826) cost the kingdom Assam, Arakan, and Tenasserim by the Treaty of Yandabo; the second (1852) took Lower Burma; and the third (1885) took everything. In November 1885 British forces occupied Mandalay, deposed King Thibaw - the last Burmese king - and annexed the whole country into the British Raj.
para4: The annexation of 1885 ended a millennium of Burmese monarchy, and the last dynasty's fall is remembered in Myanmar as a national wound. Burma became a province of British India, and guerrilla resistance to the occupation smouldered for years in the forests and hills. The Konbaung legacy - Mandalay's palace, the administrative state, and the memory of resistance - still stands at the heart of Burmese national identity.

title: The Maratha Confederacy
titleline: The Maratha Confederacy - The History Web
para1: The Maratha Confederacy. The Maratha Confederacy (1674-1818) was the power that broke the Mughal Empire - a Hindu warrior state from the western Deccan that grew, in a single century, from a mountain revolt into the master of a third of the Indian subcontinent. Its founder was Shivaji, the legendary guerrilla king who defied both the Sultanate of Bijapur and the Mughals of Aurangzeb to found 'Hindavi Swarajya' - self-rule - crowned Chhatrapati in 1674. Aurangzeb spent the last quarter-century of his reign trying to crush the Marathas and bled his empire white in the attempt.
para2: After Aurangzeb's death in 1707 the Maratha flood swept north under the Peshwas - the hereditary prime ministers at Pune who became the state's real rulers. Peshwa Bajirao I expanded the Maratha realm deep into northern India; by 1737 the Marathas, while still nominally acknowledging the Mughal emperor, in practice controlled Mughal politics. The confederacy took its mature form: the Peshwa at Pune leading four great independent Maratha houses - the Scindia of Gwalior, the Holkar of Indore, the Bhonsle of Nagpur, and the Gaekwad of Baroda - ruling some two and a half million square kilometers.
para3: The high tide broke at Panipat: in 1761 the Durrani Empire of Afghanistan crushed the Maratha army at Panipat. Yet within ten years Peshwa Madhavrao I had recovered most of the lost ground. What the Afghans could not do, the Marathas did to themselves: after the Peshwa's authority collapsed in civil strife, the defeated Peshwa Baji Rao II threw himself on British protection in 1802.
para4: That was the end. The great houses resisted the Company's encroachment in the Second and Third Anglo-Maratha Wars, and by 1818 the confederacy was destroyed, its lands absorbed into British India. The last power that could have built an Indian empire from within was gone - and the road to the British Raj lay open.

title: The Meiji Restoration
titleline: The Meiji Restoration - The History Web
para1: The Meiji Restoration. The Meiji Restoration of 1868 was the moment Japan reinvented itself - the fastest and most complete national transformation of the modern age. Fifteen years after Commodore Perry's black ships had forced Japan open, the samurai of the Satsuma and Choshu domains overthrew the Tokugawa shogunate and 'restored' the fifteen-year-old Emperor Meiji to power on 3 January 1868, promising in the Charter Oath to seek knowledge throughout the world.
para2: The young leaders around the emperor - mostly lower-ranking samurai in their thirties - dismantled the old world in a single generation. They abolished the feudal domains (1871), ended the samurai class and its privileges, created a national conscript army (1873), and sent the Iwakura Mission around the world to study the West. Railways, telegraphs, banks, factories, and a modern education system followed with astonishing speed.
para3: The transformation met resistance - most famously the Satsuma Rebellion of 1877, when the last great samurai uprising was crushed by the new conscript army it had helped create. (An earlier stand by Tokugawa loyalists, including a short-lived 'Republic of Ezo' in Hokkaido, had already failed in the Boshin War.) By 1889 Japan had the Meiji Constitution and an elected parliament and by 1905 - when it defeated Russia - it had become the first non-Western modern great power, with an empire of its own in Korea and Taiwan.
para4: The Meiji Restoration saved Japan from the fate of China - but it also turned Japan into an empire. The same drive that built the railways and warships carried Japan into wars with China (1894-95) and Russia (1904-05), the annexation of Korea (1910), and into the global struggle of the First World War, from which Japan emerged holding Germany's former Pacific islands. Modern Japan was born in 1868.

title: The Ming Dynasty
titleline: The Ming Dynasty - The History Web
para1: The Ming Dynasty. The Ming dynasty (1368-1644) was the last native Han dynasty to rule China - and for two and a half centuries one of the largest, richest, and most ordered states on earth. It rose from the wreckage of Mongol rule: Zhu Yuanzhang, a penniless peasant and former Buddhist monk, fought his way from the Red Turban rebellions to the throne, driving the Yuan back to the steppe and founding the Ming at Nanjing in 1368.
para2: As the Hongwu Emperor, Zhu tried to freeze China into a stable rural order: self-sufficient villages, a million-man standing army, the world's largest dockyards, and a rigid hierarchy of princes and scholar-officials. His son, the Yongle Emperor, seized the throne in 1402 and made Beijing the capital, building the Forbidden City, restoring the Grand Canal - and launching the extraordinary treasure voyages of Admiral Zheng He, whose giant fleets sailed the Indian Ocean to Arabia and East Africa seven times between 1405 and 1433.
para3: Then China turned inward. After the emperor himself was captured by the Mongols at Tumu in 1449, the voyages stopped, the navy rotted, and forced labor rebuilt the Great Wall into the stone form we know today. Yet the economy boomed: with perhaps 160 to 200 million people, Ming China fed itself on new American crops - maize, potatoes, chilies - and ran on a flood of American silver that poured in through European trade at Macau, making Chinese porcelain and silk the world's most desired goods.
para4: The silver also killed it. When the global silver supply faltered in the 1630s, taxes became unpayable just as the Little Ice Age brought famine and epidemic. Rebel armies under Li Zicheng took Beijing in April 1644; the last Ming emperor hanged himself, and the Manchu Qing swept in from the northeast to take the throne. Ming loyalists held out in the south until 1662, but the dynasty's age - the China of the Great Wall, the Forbidden City, and the blue-and-white vase - was over.

title: The Mughal Empire
titleline: The Mughal Empire - The History Web
para1: The Mughal Empire. The Mughal Empire (1526-1857) was the last great imperial power of pre-colonial India - at its height ruling most of the Indian subcontinent. It was founded in 1526 by Babur, a Timurid prince from the Fergana Valley, who defeated the Sultan of Delhi, Ibrahim Lodi, at the First Battle of Panipat. His son Humayun lost the new empire to the Afghan Sher Shah Suri and fled to Persia, but returned in triumph in 1555; after his accidental death the next year, his young son Akbar inherited the throne.
para2: Akbar (r. 1556-1605) made the conquest an empire: he extended Mughal rule over almost the whole subcontinent north of the Godavari, built a centralized administration and a silver currency, taxed the land through a regulated revenue system, and won over the Hindu Rajput elites with office and alliance. His court experimented with religious dialogue - even a new imperial cult, the Din-i Ilahi. Under his grandson Shah Jahan, the empire reached its architectural apogee: the Taj Mahal, the Red Fort, and Fatehpur Sikri remain among the wonders of the world, and Mughal peace made 17th-century India an expanding economic giant feeding Europe's hunger for its textiles and goods.
para3: The empire reached its greatest extent under Aurangzeb (r. 1658-1707) - and broke under the strain. His endless Deccan wars exhausted the treasury; after his death the empire hollowed out with astonishing speed: Nader Shah of Persia sacked Delhi in 1739 and carried off the Peacock Throne, the Marathas and provincial dynasties carved up the provinces, and by 1760 the emperor ruled little beyond Delhi itself, a pensioner in all but name of whoever held the city - increasingly, the British.
para4: The end came in 1857: when the great rebellion against the East India Company was crushed, the last Mughal, the aged poet-emperor Bahadur Shah II, was deposed and exiled, and the British Crown assumed direct rule of India. The Mughal legacy is India itself - its administration, its cuisine and language, and the monuments, from Humayun's Tomb to the Taj, that the whole world comes to see.

title: The Opium Wars & Century of Humiliation
titleline: The Opium Wars & Century of Humiliation - The History Web
para1: The Opium Wars and the Century of Humiliation. The Opium Wars (1839-1842 and 1856-1860) were the two conflicts that cracked China open to the West - and began the period Chinese remember as the 'century of humiliation.' Their cause was a drug trade. China sold tea, silk, and porcelain to Britain for silver, and British merchants - above all the East India Company, growing opium in Bengal - reversed the flow by smuggling opium into China by the thousands of chests a year, addicting millions and draining the empire's silver.
para2: When the Daoguang Emperor's commissioner Lin Zexu seized and destroyed 20,000 chests of British opium at Canton in 1839, Britain answered with gunboats. The Royal Navy's steam-powered warships outclassed the Qing forces, and the 1842 Treaty of Nanking - the first of the 'unequal treaties' - forced China to cede Hong Kong, pay 21 million dollars in reparations, and open five treaty ports including Shanghai to foreign trade. France and America soon extracted the same terms.
para3: The Second Opium War (1856-1860) went further: Britain and France, using a minor incident over the ship Arrow as a pretext, fought their way to Beijing itself, looted and burned the emperor's Old Summer Palace, and imposed the Treaties of Tianjin and the Convention of Peking - opening ten more ports, legalizing the opium trade, allowing Christian missionaries into the interior, and ceding the Kowloon peninsula.
para4: The wars exposed the Qing empire's weakness to the world - and to itself. For a century afterward, foreign powers dictated terms on Chinese soil, while rebellions and reform movements tore at the dynasty from within. The memory of those decades - taught to every Chinese schoolchild as the century of humiliation - still shapes how China sees the West and itself.

title: The Ottoman Empire
titleline: The Ottoman Empire - The History Web
para1: The Ottoman Empire. The Ottoman Empire (c. 1299-1922) was one of the longest-lived empires in world history: for over six centuries the House of Osman ruled from Constantinople at the crossroads of Europe and the Middle East, at its height holding lands on three continents. It began around 1299 as a tiny beylik on the Byzantine frontier in northwestern Anatolia, founded by the Turkoman leader Osman I. His son Orhan took Bursa in 1326; by mid-century the Ottomans were in the Balkans, breaking Serbian power at Kosovo in 1389 - and even catastrophe, Timur's crushing victory at Ankara in 1402, only delayed them for a generation.
para2: The empire's two defining conquests came a century apart. In 1453 Mehmed II took Constantinople, ending the thousand-year Byzantine Empire and making the city his capital; in 1517 Selim I destroyed the Mamluks, and the Ottoman sultans assumed the title of caliph, leaders of the Islamic world. Under Suleiman the Magnificent (r. 1520-1566) - conqueror of Belgrade, victor of Mohacs, master of Baghdad - the empire became a global power, its laws and its armies the envy and terror of Europe. Its millions of Christian and Jewish subjects lived under the millet system, managing their own communal affairs.
para3: Modern historians date the long decline from the failed second siege of Vienna in 1683. The empire fell behind Europe technologically, lost wars and provinces to Austria and Russia, and watched new Balkan nations break away. Yet the 19th century also brought serious reform - the Tanzimat era, constitutional experiments, and finally the Young Turk Revolution of 1908 - before the Balkan Wars and the First World War brought the end: defeat, the Arab Revolt, genocide against Armenians, Assyrians, and Greeks, and Allied partition.
para4: The sultanate was abolished in November 1922; the Republic of Turkey rose from its ruins under Mustafa Kemal Ataturk in 1923, and the caliphate itself was abolished in 1924. The Ottoman imprint endures everywhere its borders ran: in the nations of the Balkans and the Arab world, in Istanbul's skyline, and in the modern Republic of Turkey itself.

title: The Qajar Empire
titleline: The Qajar Empire - The History Web
para1: The Qajar Empire. The Qajar dynasty, established in 1789, ruled Iran through the age of European empire - a reign of glittering courts and shrinking borders, in which Iran lost the Caucasus to Russia, escaped colonization by a hair's breadth, and ended by giving itself a constitution. It was founded by the formidable Agha Mohammad Khan, chieftain of the Qajar tribe, who defeated every rival of the Zand and Afsharid age, made his capital at Tehran, and was crowned Shah in 1796 - only to be assassinated the following year.
para2: His nephew Fath-Ali Shah inherited a fatal contest: Russia was advancing into the Caucasus, which Iran had ruled for centuries. Two disastrous wars settled it. By the Treaty of Gulistan (1813) Iran ceded Georgia, Dagestan, and most of Azerbaijan; by the Treaty of Turkmenchay (1828), after Russia took Tabriz, it gave up the entire South Caucasus, and the border was fixed on the Aras River - where it remains. Iran's attempt to recover Herat in Afghanistan ended with the Treaty of Paris (1857), dictated by Britain.
para3: The long 19th century was the era of the Great Game: Russia pressing from the north, Britain from the Gulf and India, both extracting concessions while Qajar Iran maintained a precarious independence. Pressure produced change: in 1906 the Constitutional Revolution forced the Shah to grant the National Consultative Assembly - the Majlis - and Iran became a constitutional monarchy. The great powers answered in 1907 by formally dividing the country into Russian and British spheres of influence.
para4: The dynasty did not long survive the war's aftermath. Iran in 1921 was prostrate: partly occupied by foreign troops, its treasury empty, its governments rotating helplessly. That February an obscure Cossack Brigade officer, Reza Khan, marched on Tehran with the journalist-politician Sayyid Zia al-Din Tabatabai and seized power in a nearly bloodless coup. Zia soon fell, but Reza Khan rose: war minister, commander-in-chief, and by 1923 prime minister, while the young Ahmad Shah lingered in Europe. By 1924 the Qajar crown still sat in Tehran - but the soldier who really ruled Iran was already being spoken of as its next king.

title: The Qing Dynasty
titleline: The Qing Dynasty - The History Web
para1: The Qing Dynasty. The Qing dynasty (1644-1912) was China's last imperial dynasty - and its largest. Founded by the Manchus, a people of the northeast whose leader Nurhaci had unified the Jurchen tribes into the Later Jin state in 1616, the Qing seized Beijing in 1644 when the Ming general Wu Sangui opened the Great Wall's Shanhai Pass to them, then ground down forty years of resistance to complete the conquest of China by 1683.
para2: Under three extraordinary long-lived emperors the Qing reached its zenith. The Kangxi Emperor (r. 1661-1722) consolidated the empire and patronized Confucian scholarship; the Qianlong Emperor (r. 1735-1796) pushed its frontiers deep into Central Asia, destroying the Dzungar Khanate and adding Xinjiang, Mongolia, and Tibet. At its height the Qing ruled the most territory of any dynasty in Chinese history - in 1790 the fourth-largest empire the world had yet seen - and the most people: over 400 million.
para3: The nineteenth century brought collapse from without and within. Defeat in the Opium Wars forced China open to unequal treaties, foreign treaty ports, and the 'century of humiliation'; the Taiping Rebellion (1850-1864) and other revolts killed more than 20 million people; and defeat by Japan in 1895 showed that even Asia no longer feared the dragon throne. Reform came too late and too slowly.
para4: The end came in 1911-1912: the Xinhai Revolution swept the provinces, and in February 1912 the last emperor - the child Puyi - abdicated, ending not just a dynasty but two thousand years of Chinese monarchy. The Republic of China took over an empire the Qing had assembled, and modern China's borders are still essentially the ones the Manchu emperors drew.

title: The Russian Conquest of Central Asia
titleline: The Russian Conquest of Central Asia - The History Web
para1: The Russian Conquest of Central Asia. The Russian conquest of Central Asia (1717-1895) turned the map of a continent: in a century and a half, the Tsar's armies absorbed the steppe of the Kazakh khans, the oasis khanates of Bukhara, Khiva, and Kokand, and the Turkmen desert - creating Russian Turkestan and bringing the Russian Empire to the borders of Afghanistan, Persia, and China. It was the Central Asian half of the Great Game.
para2: The steppe came first. Through the 18th and 19th centuries Russia pushed its line of forts deeper into the Kazakh grasslands; the abolition of the Kazakh khanate in the 1820s provoked Kenesary Qasymuly's ten-year rebellion, crushed by 1847. Fort by fort - the Turgay, the Irgiz, Fort Raim on the Syr Darya - the Russians advanced, completing the Syr-Darya Line by 1864.
para3: The main event followed at once: in 1864-1868 the Russians drove south into the settled zone. Tashkent fell in June 1865 after Chernayev's night storm of its walls; Samarkand followed in 1868. The Khanate of Kokand was penned into the Fergana Valley and annexed outright in 1876; the Emirate of Bukhara and the Khanate of Khiva survived only as Russian protectorates. The pattern was the same everywhere: Russian breech-loading rifles and artillery shattering armies many times their size.
para4: The conquest ended in the 1880s-90s with the absorption of the Turkmen lands and the fixing of the Afghan frontier: Russia and Britain, rivals in the Great Game, agreed to leave Afghanistan as a neutral buffer between their empires. Russian rule was shaken but not broken by the great revolt of 1916, when the tsar's decree drafting Muslims for war labor provoked uprisings from the steppe to Fergana, suppressed with terrible violence. The conquest had created a new order - Russian Turkestan, with its railways, cotton and settler towns - that the fall of the empire itself would only reshape.

title: The Russian Conquest of the Caucasus
titleline: The Russian Conquest of the Caucasus - The History Web
para1: The Russian Conquest of the Caucasus. The Russian conquest of the Caucasus was one of the longest and bloodiest colonial wars of the 19th century - a half-century struggle (1817-1864) that brought the mountain peoples of the North Caucasus under the Tsar at a terrible human cost. Russia's advance began with the kingdoms south of the mountains: in 1801 it annexed the Georgian kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti, and two victorious wars with Qajar Persia - sealed by the treaties of Gulistan (1813) and Turkmenchay (1828) - gave it the whole South Caucasus, from Dagestan to Armenia.
para2: The mountains themselves were another matter. The Caucasian War pitted the Russian Imperial Army and Cossack settlers against the Adyghe (Circassians), Chechens, Dagestanis, Abazins, and Ubykhs. In the east, the mountaineers found a leader of genius in Imam Shamil, who from 1834 held the empire at bay for a quarter-century - in 1843 capturing nearly every Russian outpost in Avaria in a single month, in 1845 withstanding Prince Vorontsov's great offensive. It took an army of 250,000 under General Baryatinsky to break the resistance; Shamil was captured in 1859 and exiled to central Russia.
para3: In the west, the war against the Circassians continued to 1864 - and ended in catastrophe for its victims. The conquest was accompanied by what is now called the Circassian genocide: the massacre, expulsion, and exile of the Circassian people to the Ottoman Empire. Kabardia's population fell from some 350,000 before the war to 50,000; at the Ottoman port of Samsun alone, up to 110,000 refugees huddled in camps where hundreds died daily. Cossack and Russian colonists were settled on the confiscated lands, remaking the region's ethnic map. On 21 May 1864, Tsar Alexander II declared the war over.
para4: The conquest left deep scars - a Circassian diaspora scattered across the Middle East, and grievances that erupted again in the 20th century. It also entered world literature: Pushkin's 'Prisoner of the Caucasus,' Lermontov's poems, and Tolstoy's tales of war were all born in those mountains.

title: The Safavid Empire
titleline: The Safavid Empire - The History Web
para1: The Safavid Empire. The Safavid Empire (1501-1736) is where modern Iran begins - the dynasty that made Iran a Shia Muslim nation and one of the great 'gunpowder empires' of the early modern world. In 1501 the young Shah Ismail I, carried to power by his fanatical Qizilbash - the 'red-head' Turkoman tribesmen - proclaimed Twelver Shi'ism the official religion of his empire. It was one of the great turning points in the history of Islam: Iran, until then largely Sunni, became the heartland of the Shia, and the sectarian geography of the Middle East was fixed into our own time.
para2: The early shahs warred constantly with the Sunni Ottomans and Uzbeks on their borders. Under Shah Tahmasp the empire began a profound transformation: to break the Qizilbash's grip on the army, the shahs imported hundreds of thousands of Georgians, Circassians, and Armenians from the Caucasus as ghulams - royal slaves trained for war and government, much like the Ottoman janissaries - who rose to the highest offices of the state.
para3: The dynasty's zenith came under Shah Abbas the Great (r. 1588-1629). He completed the ghulam army, built an artillery corps with European help, moved his capital to Isfahan, and revived the Silk Road through Iran, opening direct trade with England and the Netherlands in silk, carpets, and textiles. Isfahan under Abbas became one of the showpieces of the world, and Safavid Persia an economic stronghold between East and West, its court a rich mix of Turkoman lords, Persian bureaucrats, and Caucasian soldiers and courtiers.
para4: The end came with shocking speed: in 1722 Afghan tribesmen besieged and took Isfahan itself, and the once-mighty empire collapsed. The conqueror Nader Shah drove out the Afghans and briefly restored the Safavids as puppets before taking the throne himself in 1736. But the Safavid imprint on Iran was permanent: the Shia faith, the efficient state, and the architectural glories of Isfahan remain the dynasty's living legacy.

title: The Spanish East Indies
titleline: The Spanish East Indies - The History Web
para1: The Spanish East Indies. The Spanish East Indies - Spain's Asian empire, centered on the Philippines - lasted 333 years, from 1565 to 1898, the longest European colonial rule in Southeast Asia. Ferdinand Magellan had reached the islands in 1521 and died at Mactan; the conquest itself began in 1565, when Miguel Lopez de Legazpi sailed from Mexico, took Cebu, and in 1571 founded Manila as the capital. The whole archipelago was named for King Philip II of Spain.
para2: The Philippines were ruled from across the Pacific: for over 250 years the islands belonged to the Viceroyalty of New Spain, governed from Mexico City, and were tied to America by the Manila galleon - the great annual ships that crossed the Pacific between Manila and Acapulco for two and a half centuries, carrying Mexican silver east and Chinese silk, porcelain, and spices west, in one of history's first truly global trade routes.
para3: Spanish rule was thin - a small Spanish population ruling through friars and local chiefs - but its cultural impact was enormous: it converted most of the islands to Catholicism, built towns and universities, and welded hundreds of scattered chiefdoms into a single colony. The colony was even a financial drain on Spain, kept alive by an annual silver subsidy from Mexico.
para4: The end came in 1896-1898: a Philippine revolution rose against Spain, and then the United States defeated Spain in the Spanish-American War. By the Treaty of Paris of December 1898, Spain sold the Philippines to the United States for twenty million dollars. Three centuries of Spanish rule ended - and the Filipinos, who had already proclaimed their independence, found themselves fighting a new colonizer instead.

title: The Tanzimat Era
titleline: The Tanzimat Era - The History Web
para1: The Tanzimat Era. The Tanzimat - the 'Reorganization' (1839-1876) - was the Ottoman Empire's great attempt to save itself by reinventing itself: four decades in which reforming sultans and statesmen tried to build a modern, centralized, law-governed state on European lines, while holding a multinational empire together. It began on November 3, 1839, when the young Sultan Abdulmejid I issued the Edict of Gulhane, promising all his subjects - Muslim, Christian, and Jew alike - security of life, honor, and property, fair taxation and conscription, and public trials, and abolishing the notorious system of tax farming.
para2: The driving force was a generation of reformist statesmen - Mustafa Resid Pasha, Ali Pasha, and Fuad Pasha - who had served as ambassadors in London and Paris and believed European institutions could restore Ottoman power. Under them the empire gained ministries, secular Nizamiye courts alongside the religious ones, a modern school system capped by the Darulfunun, its first telegraph lines and railways, and codified laws for the millets, the empire's religious communities. The Imperial Reform Edict of 1856 went further still, proclaiming full legal equality for non-Muslims - the principle of Ottomanism, one citizenship for all the sultan's subjects.
para3: Reform had its price. The changes met resistance from conservative clerics, sharpened ethnic tensions in the Balkans, and were paid for with foreign loans - the first borrowed in 1858 to finance the Crimean War - that saddled the empire with crippling debt. Yet the momentum carried to its logical end: in 1876, amid the Great Eastern Crisis, Midhat Pasha and his allies deposed Sultan Abdulaziz and proclaimed the Ottoman constitution, opening the First Constitutional Era.
para4: The Tanzimat's legacy is still contested: some historians credit it with creating a powerful modern state and a new Ottoman identity; others argue it accelerated the empire's fragmentation. What is certain is that it transformed the empire's government, law, and daily life - and that every later Ottoman and Turkish reform, down to the Republic itself, built on its foundations.

title: The Tokugawa Shogunate (Edo Period)
titleline: The Tokugawa Shogunate (Edo Period) - The History Web
para1: The Tokugawa Shogunate (Edo Period). The Tokugawa shogunate (1603-1868) - the Edo period - was 265 years of peace, order, and isolation that made Japan what it is. It began when Tokugawa Ieyasu won the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600, ending a century of civil war, and took the title of shogun in 1603. For two and a half centuries, the Tokugawa clan ruled Japan from Edo Castle - the future Tokyo - while the emperor remained a powerless figurehead in Kyoto.
para2: The shoguns built one of history's most tightly ordered societies. The samurai warrior class stood at the top of a fixed four-class hierarchy; the great lords (daimyo) governed their domains but were forced to spend alternate years at Edo, keeping their families as hostages. Christianity was banned, and under the sakoku ('closed country') edicts of the 1630s, Japan shut itself off: no Japanese could leave, and foreigners could enter only through one Dutch trading post at Nagasaki.
para3: Peace transformed the country. Edo grew into one of the largest cities in the world; the merchant class rose on rice, silk, and credit; and townspeople created a brilliant urban culture - kabuki theater, ukiyo-e prints, haiku poetry, and the pleasure quarters of the 'floating world.' A samurai-dominated state had produced a merchant's civilization.
para4: The isolation ended in 1853, when American Commodore Perry's 'black ships' steamed into Edo Bay and demanded Japan open its ports. The shogunate, unable to resist, signed the Kanagawa Treaty of 1854 - and the crisis shattered its authority. Samurai reformers rallied around the emperor, and in 1868 the last shogun fell in the Meiji Restoration. Japan emerged from two centuries of seclusion determined to catch up with the world - and did so in a single generation.

title: The Tulip Period & Early Reforms
titleline: The Tulip Period & Early Reforms - The History Web
para1: The Tulip Period and Early Reforms. The Tulip Period (1718-1730) was the Ottoman Empire's first opening to the West - a dozen years of peace, flowers, and fountains that began the empire's long, reluctant transformation. It opened with the Treaty of Passarowitz in 1718, which ended a generation of war with Austria, and it took its name from the tulip craze that swept the court of Sultan Ahmed III: tulips filled the palaces, the gardens, the fabrics, and the poetry of Istanbul's elite.
para2: The man of the age was the Grand Vizier, Nevsehirli Damat Ibrahim Pasha, the sultan's son-in-law. Under his guidance the empire oriented itself outwards: trade and industry were promoted, and Ottoman public buildings took on Western European elements for the first time - the beginning of Ottoman Baroque architecture. Most momentous of all, the 1720s saw the establishment of the first Ottoman-language printing press, more than two centuries after printing had transformed Europe.
para3: But the elegance rested on a fragile base. The luxury of the court enraged the capital's soldiers and preachers, and in September 1730 the Patrona Halil revolt swept Ibrahim Pasha and the Tulip Age away. Yet the question the period had posed - how could the empire catch up with Europe? - would not go away. Sultan Selim III (r. 1789-1807) made the first major attempt to modernize the army; the Janissary corps, jealous of its privileges, revolted and destroyed him.
para4: The answer came in blood: Selim's successor, the dynamic Mahmud II, eliminated the Janissary corps in 1826, removing the greatest obstacle to reform and clearing the road to the Tanzimat. The Tulip Period's brief flowering had shown that Ottoman renewal was possible; the destruction of the Janissaries showed what it would cost.

title: The Uzbek Khanate
titleline: The Uzbek Khanate - The History Web
para1: The Uzbek Khanate. The Uzbek Khanate was the power that remade Central Asia at the close of the Timurid age - and its successor states, the khanates of Bukhara, Khiva, and Kokand, ruled the oases of Turkestan until the Russian Empire swallowed them in the 19th century. The Uzbeks were steppe nomads of the Golden Horde's successor world, welded into a khanate in the 15th century by the Chinggisid prince Abu'l-Khayr. His grandson Muhammad Shaybani led them to empire: in 1500-1501 he conquered Transoxiana - Samarkand, Bukhara, Tashkent, and Balkh - from the last Timurids, founding the Khanate of Bukhara.
para2: Under the Shaybanids and their successors the Janids (from 1599), Bukhara - made the permanent capital by Abdullah Khan II in 1562 - gave its name to the state, ruling Transoxiana's ancient cities of Samarkand, Tashkent, and Balkh. In 1740 the conqueror Nader Shah overran the khanate; after his death the Manghit clan seized power, and in 1785 Shah Murad replaced the khanate with the Emirate of Bukhara - its rulers taking the title emir since, not being descended from Genghis Khan, they could not claim the title of khan.
para3: To the west, in the ancient land of Khwarazm, the Khanate of Khiva (1511-1920) ruled from the walls of Khiva, surviving as an Afsharid vassal in the 1740s and later as a Russian protectorate from 1873. To the east, the Khanate of Kokand (1709-1876) rose in the fertile Fergana Valley, fought off Dzungar invasions, and grew rich on irrigated agriculture and the trade between India and Russia - until Russian armies abolished it in 1876.
para4: The khanates' world ended with the Russian conquest of Central Asia: Kokand annexed in 1876, Khiva and Bukhara reduced to protectorates, and both finally extinguished in 1920. But the Uzbek name they carried - from Abu'l-Khayr's steppe horde - lives on in modern Uzbekistan.

title: The Durrani Empire
titleline: The Durrani Empire - The History Web
para1: The Durrani Empire. The Durrani Empire (1747-1823) created Afghanistan. When the Persian conqueror Nader Shah was assassinated in 1747, his Afghan cavalry commander Ahmad Khan Abdali - a 25-year-old chief of the Sadozai clan - was chosen king by a jirga of the Afghan tribes at Kandahar, taking the title Durr-i-Durran ('Pearl of Pearls'), from which his Durrani dynasty and the renamed Durrani (formerly Abdali) tribal confederacy took their names.
para2: Ahmad Shah Durrani built in twenty-five years what his founder-kingdom became: from Kandahar he took Kabul, Herat and the Afghan highlands, then campaigned ceaselessly - into Khorasan, Central Asia, Kashmir, and above all India, which he invaded nine times. His climactic victory came at the Third Battle of Panipat (1761), where his Afghan and allied Muslim forces annihilated the Maratha army - one of the largest battles of the 18th century - halting Maratha expansion and reshaping India's future, though he could not hold the Gangetic plain himself.
para3: Ahmad Shah was more than a raider: a poet in Pashto and Persian, he welded the fractious Pashtun tribes into a state, fixed its capitals at Kandahar and Kabul, and is honored by Afghans as Ahmad Shah Baba, the father of the nation. At his death in 1772 the empire stretched from the Oxus to the Arabian Sea and from Persia to the Indus.
para4: His successors squandered it in fratricidal wars between the Sadozai and Barakzai clans, losing Punjab and Kashmir to the Sikhs and Sindh and Baluchistan to local rulers; in 1823 the last Sadozai shah lost Kabul to the Barakzai Dost Muhammad Khan, and the empire contracted to its Afghan core - but the idea of Afghanistan, as a Durrani state between Persia and India, survived into the modern nation.

title: The Emirate of Bukhara
titleline: The Emirate of Bukhara - The History Web
para1: The Emirate of Bukhara. The Emirate of Bukhara (1785-1920) was the last Central Asian state of the ancient city of Bukhara, ruled by the Uzbek Manghit dynasty. When the Janid khanate collapsed, the Manghit ataliq Muhammad Rahim murdered his rivals and took the throne; his successors assumed the religious title emir, ruling Bukhara's shrunken territories - the Zeravshan valley, Samarkand (lost and partly recovered), and vassals toward the Pamirs - as a staunchly Sunni, Persian-speaking court.
para2: Nineteenth-century Bukhara was famous and notorious in equal measure: its medressas - hundreds of them - still drew students from across the Islamic world; its bazaars traded astrakhan, cotton and slaves; and its emirs - above all the capricious Nasrullah Khan (r. 1827-1860), the 'Butcher Emir' - executed British envoys (Stoddart and Conolly, 1842, in the shadow of the Ark fortress) and ruled through fear, while the court glittered with poetry and intrigue.
para3: Russia closed in: after taking Samarkand (1868), Russia made Emir Muzaffar a vassal, annexing half the emirate; the remainder survived as a protectorate, its emirs - isolated, reactionary, contemptuous of the reforming Jadid intellectuals Bukhara itself produced - drifting into the 20th century as a museum-piece despotism under Russian guarantee.
para4: In 1920 the last emir, Alim Khan, fled before the Red Army's assault on the Ark; the short-lived Bukharan People's Soviet Republic that replaced him was absorbed into the new Soviet order in 1924, and the emirate's ancient lands were divided among new republics. Bukhara's emirate left the city's matchless medieval core - the Kalyan minaret, the Ark, the Lab-i Hauz - intact, a monument to the world Russia ended.

title: The Khanate of Khiva
titleline: The Khanate of Khiva - The History Web
para1: The Khanate of Khiva. The Khanate of Khiva (1511-1920) ruled Khwarezm, the oasis at the Amu Darya's delta, for four centuries under Uzbek dynasties of Chinggisid descent. Founded when the Uzbek Ilbars Khan seized Khwarezm from the Safavids, the khanate lived from the oasis's canals and from the slave trade - its raiders carried off Persian, Russian and Kazakh captives for the markets of Khiva and Bukhara - a trade that drew Russian and Persian punishment expeditions for three hundred years.
para2: Khiva's 19th-century khans of the Qungrat dynasty presided over a late flowering: Muhammad Rahim Khan I (r. 1806-1825) subdued the steppe tribes and patronized letters, and under his successors Khiva became a center of Chagatai-Turkic literature and historiography - the court poets and historians Munis and Agahi chronicled the khanate itself - while building the city that survives today: Itchan Kala, Khiva's walled inner city with its blue-tiled Kalta Minor minaret, is a UNESCO site and the best-preserved royal city of Central Asia.
para3: Russia had failed once - the disastrous 1839-1840 winter expedition of General Perovsky lost most of its men and camels to the steppe - but by the 1860s-70s the conquest of Turkestan made Khiva's fall inevitable: in 1873 General Kaufmann's converging columns crossed the desert, took the city, and imposed a protectorate; the khan kept his throne as a Russian vassal, and the slave markets were closed at last.
para4: The protectorate staggered on until the Russian Revolution: in 1920 the Red Army deposed the last khan, and the Khorezm People's Soviet Republic - absorbed into the USSR in 1924 - divided the old khanate between Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan. Khiva's Itchan Kala preserves the khanate's whole world in sun-baked mud-brick and tile.

title: The Khanate of Kokand
titleline: The Khanate of Kokand - The History Web
para1: The Khanate of Kokand. The Khanate of Kokand (1709-1876) was the youngest, most dynamic, and most expansionist of Central Asia's Uzbek khanates, ruling the rich Ferghana Valley. Founded by Shah Rukh of the Ming tribe when Bukhara's hold on Ferghana slipped, Kokand rose in the early 19th century under khans like Alim and Omar Khan and the poet-king Umar's widow Nadira, building an empire from Tashkent to the Pamirs on the valley's cotton, silk, horses and the caravan trade between Russia, Kashgar and India.
para2: Kokand's khans were builders and patrons: Omar Khan's court drew poets and chroniclers; the khans raised the great madrasas and palaces of Kokand city and forts across the steppe; and their state was famously cosmopolitan - Uzbek rulers, Tajik clerks and merchants, Kyrgyz and Kazakh cavalry, and a stream of envoys, spies and travelers from Russia, Britain (the Great Game ran through Kokand) and China.
para3: But Kokand was chronically unstable - palace coups, wars with Bukhara, and revolts of the Kyrgyz nomads - and Russia was coming. After taking Tashkent (1865), Russia reduced the khanate to a protectorate (1868), and when the unpopular Khudoyar Khan's exactions sparked the great Ferghana uprising of 1875, Russia used the chaos to annex the khanate outright in 1876, making Ferghana a province of Turkestan. The last resistance flickered as a jihad under the pretender Pulat Khan.
para4: Kokand's legacy is Ferghana itself: the valley it organized remains Central Asia's demographic and agricultural heartland - its lands apportioned among new republics after the empire fell - and the khanate's memory fueled the 1898 Andijan uprising and the region's stubborn resistance to conquest. Its khans' palace, the Khudoyar Khan Palace, still stands in Kokand.

title: The First and Second Saudi States
titleline: The First and Second Saudi States - The History Web
para1: The First and Second Saudi States. The First Saudi State (1744-1818) was born of an alliance that still shapes Arabia: in 1744 Muhammad ibn Saud, emir of the oasis town of Diriyah, joined his sword to the religious mission of Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab, whose austere call to pure monotheism condemned the veneration of saints, tombs and trees sweeping the peninsula. Saudis supplied the army; the preacher supplied the creed; and in two generations their state conquered most of Arabia.
para2: From Diriyah, the Saudi-Wahhabi forces subdued Najd, then broke the power of the sharifs: they took al-Ahsa, raided into Ottoman Iraq - sacking Karbala in 1802 and shocking the Muslim world - and seized Mecca (1803) and Medina (1804), closing the holy cities to the pilgrimage caravans and purging their shrines. The Ottoman sultan, unable to answer from Baghdad, unleashed Muhammad Ali of Egypt, whose modernized army under his son Ibrahim Pasha fought its way into Najd and destroyed Diriyah in 1818; the first emir, Abdullah, was sent to Istanbul and beheaded.
para3: Within years the Saudi house rose again: Turki ibn Abdullah re-established the emirate at Riyadh (1824), and the Second Saudi State (1824-1891) ruled Najd for two generations - notably under Turki's son Faisal, whose long reign reasserted Saudi power from the Gulf to the Rub al-Khali - before dynastic feuds after Faisal's death let the rival Rashidi emirs of Hail take Riyadh (1891) and drive the Sauds into exile in Kuwait.
para4: The exile was brief: in 1902 Abd al-Aziz ibn Saud retook Riyadh in a famous night raid, founding the Third Saudi State that became the modern Kingdom of Saudi Arabia. Diriyah's ruins - now restored as a UNESCO site - and the enduring Saudi-Wahhabi compact remain the foundation stones of the Saudi state.

title: The Omani Empire
titleline: The Omani Empire - The History Web
para1: The Omani Empire. The Omani Empire (1698-1856) made Oman the greatest maritime power of the western Indian Ocean. After expelling the Portuguese from Muscat (1650), the Ya'rubi imams took the war overseas: in 1698 an Omani fleet stormed Fort Jesus and drove Portugal from Mombasa, beginning Oman's long rule over the Swahili coast. Under the Al Bu Said dynasty - founded 1744 and reigning in Oman to this day - the sultanate grew rich on Gulf trade, dates, and the sea.
para2: The empire's architect was Sayyid Said bin Sultan (r. 1806-1856), 'Said the Great': he made a treaty of commerce with the United States (1833) - America's first with an Arab state - and with Britain and France; built a navy of East-Indiamen that sailed to Zanzibar, Bombay and beyond; and progressively shifted his court to Zanzibar, the clove island he and his Omani Arab settlers transformed into the clove capital of the world and the hub of the East African ivory and slave trades. By 1840 Zanzibar, not Muscat, was his capital, and his writ ran from the Makran coast to Lake Tanganyika.
para3: Omani Zanzibar was a cosmopolitan Arab-Swahili court: Stone Town's carved doors and palaces (the Beit al-Ajaib, 'House of Wonders') rose in Said's reign, alongside the brutal engine of its wealth - the slave markets and caravan routes deep into Africa, which British pressure slowly, and only late, closed down.
para4: At Said's death in 1856 his sons split the empire - Thuwaini taking Muscat and Oman, Majid taking Zanzibar and the coast - under British arbitration. Zanzibar passed under British protection in 1890 and its sultans reigned on over the clove island, while in Muscat the Al Bu Said faced the tribes of the interior and the imams who challenged their authority into the new century - heirs, in reduced circumstances, to the only non-European overseas empire of the 19th century.

title: The Trucial States
titleline: The Trucial States - The History Web
para1: The Trucial States. The Trucial States - the sheikhdoms of the lower Gulf linked to British treaties from 1820 - take their name from the maritime truces Britain imposed on the 'Pirate Coast'. Through the 18th century the Qawasim confederation of Ras al-Khaimah and Sharjah dominated Gulf shipping and fought a long, ambiguous war - piracy to the British, legitimate maritime struggle to the Qawasim - with the East India Company, which destroyed Ras al-Khaimah's fleet in 1819.
para2: In 1820 the sheikhs of the coast - the Qawasim of Sharjah and Ras al-Khaimah, the Bani Yas of Abu Dhabi and Dubai, and the other small sheikhdoms - signed the General Maritime Treaty with Britain, renouncing plunder and slavery at sea; the Perpetual Maritime Truce of 1853 made the peace permanent, and the sheikhdoms became the 'Trucial States'. In 1892 they accepted exclusive British protection of their foreign relations, leaving internal rule to the sheikhs - the Al Qasimi, Al Nahyan, Al Maktoum, Al Nuaimi, Al Mualla and Al Sharqi houses that rule the emirates still.
para3: For the next century the truce coast lived on the sea. Pearling was its heart: every summer thousands of divers and haulers took the great fleets of Dubai, Abu Dhabi, Sharjah and Lingeh out to the oyster banks, in a hard seasonal rhythm that organized the sheikhdoms' whole economy, while entrepot trade connected the coast to India, Persia and East Africa. The treaty system kept the peace at sea, and the British resident at Bushire - later his political agents in the sheikhdoms - settled the sheikhs' disputes and watched their foreign dealings, leaving the ruling families, the Al Qasimi, Al Nahyan, Al Maktoum and the rest, secure in their internal rule.
para4: The early twentieth century brought quiet consolidation rather than change: Dubai under the Al Maktoum grew into the coast's busiest free port after merchants moved across from Lingeh in the 1900s, and the sheikhdoms weathered the First World War on the margins of empire. By 1924 the Trucial States remained what the nineteenth century had made them - small maritime sheikhdoms under British protection, whose pearling fleets still sailed out every season as they had for generations.

title: French Mandate Syria and Lebanon
titleline: French Mandate Syria and Lebanon - The History Web
para1: French Mandate Syria and Lebanon. French rule in Syria and Lebanon began in blood. When the Ottoman Empire collapsed, the Arab Kingdom of Syria - proclaimed at Damascus in 1920 under Faisal, the Hashemite leader of the Arab Revolt - claimed the whole of geographical Syria; but at San Remo the Allied powers had already assigned Syria and Lebanon to France as a League of Nations mandate. In July 1920 General Gouraud's French army crushed the Syrian army at Maysalun and occupied Damascus; Faisal went into exile.
para2: France ruled by division: it carved the mandate into statelets - Damascus, Aleppo, the Alawite and Druze states, and the expanded 'Greater Lebanon', proclaimed in 1920 with borders drawn to give the Maronite Christians a viable state - and governed through urban notables, a bureaucracy of French officials, and soldiers recruited disproportionately from the minorities, against the hostility of an Arab nationalist majority that had expected independence after the Ottoman collapse.
para3: The early mandate years were a running contest. France abolished Faisal's institutions, imposed its currency and its advisers, and answered protest with arrests, while Syrian notables carried their case to the League of Nations in Geneva. Resentment smouldered in the countryside, above all in the Druze Jabal in the south, where the great Druze families chafed under the French officers sent to administer them. In Lebanon the new state's communities argued over its shape: many Muslims resented inclusion in a Christian-led Greater Lebanon, while the Maronite patriarchate defended the enlarged borders.
para4: By 1924 the mandate was four years old and firmly in French hands, but its settlement was visibly provisional: the borders France had drawn, the sectarian balance it had codified, and the nationalism it had suppressed were all still in place, and the tensions of the early 1920s - in Damascus, in the Druze Jabal, and between Lebanon's communities - were already gathering toward confrontation.

title: British Mandate Iraq and Palestine
titleline: British Mandate Iraq and Palestine - The History Web
para1: British Mandate Iraq and Palestine. Britain's mandates in Iraq and Palestine were invented at the end of the First World War from three Ottoman provinces and a set of contradictory wartime promises. Britain had conquered Mesopotamia in a hard campaign against the Ottomans (1914-1918) and taken Jerusalem in 1917; at San Remo in 1920 the League of Nations confirmed British mandates over Iraq, Palestine and Transjordan - just as Britain's wartime pledges, to the Arabs in the Hussein-McMahon correspondence, to the Zionists in the Balfour Declaration of 1917, and to France at Sykes-Picot, were coming due.
para2: In Iraq, the great revolt of 1920 against British rule - tribes and towns, Sunni and Shi'a together - was crushed at heavy cost, and Britain chose indirect rule. At the Cairo Conference of 1921, Churchill and his advisers offered the Iraqi throne to Faisal, the Hashemite expelled from Syria, who was crowned in Baghdad that August; his brother Abdullah was installed in the new emirate of Transjordan east of the river, and a treaty in 1922 regularized Britain's position - bases, advisers and oil interests - behind the facade of an independent Arab kingdom.
para3: In Palestine, the mandate administered the impossible: building a Jewish national home, as the Balfour Declaration promised, within an Arab majority determined to prevent it. Arab crowds rioted in Jerusalem in 1920 and Jaffa in 1921; the Zionist movement bought land, founded settlements, and laid out the Hebrew city of Tel Aviv; and Churchill's White Paper of 1922 tried to reassure both sides at once, insisting Britain had never promised that Arab Palestine would disappear. In 1922 the League of Nations formally confirmed both mandates.
para4: By 1924 the new order was taking shape: Britain ruled Iraq through the Hashemites and Palestine through a colonial administration, a new wave of Jewish immigration - the Fourth Aliyah - was changing Palestine's towns, and the contradictions written into the mandates at their birth, Arab nationalism in Iraq and the Arab-Jewish contest in Palestine, were already visible in every institution Britain had built.

title: The Hashemite Kingdoms
titleline: The Hashemite Kingdoms - The History Web
para1: The Hashemite Kingdoms. The Hashemites - the Prophet Muhammad's clan, sharifs of Mecca for a thousand years - held power in the Hejaz and in several states created after the First World War. When Sharif Hussein launched the Arab Revolt against the Ottomans (1916) in alliance with Britain, he proclaimed himself King of the Arabs, ruling the Hejaz; his sons became the dynasts of the post-Ottoman settlement: Faisal, king of Syria for four months in 1920, expelled by France and crowned king of Iraq (1921); Abdullah, given the new emirate of Transjordan east of the river (1921).
para2: Hussein's kingdom faced mounting danger from Abd al-Aziz ibn Saud, the rising ruler of Najd. Hussein's assumption of the caliphate after the Turkish abolition of the office in March 1924 added to regional rivalries. Saudi forces captured Taif and Mecca that autumn. Hussein abdicated in favour of his son Ali, who continued to hold Jeddah. At the end of 1924, the struggle for the Hejaz was not over: the loss of Mecca did not yet mean the disappearance of Ali's kingdom.
para3: The sons' new thrones were made of different stuff. In Iraq, Faisal ruled a restive kingdom of Arabs and Kurds, Sunnis and Shi'a, balancing British advisers, tribal sheikhs and the nationalist politicians of Baghdad, while the strategic and economic prospects of the Mosul region attracted international attention. In Transjordan, Abdullah governed a poor desert emirate of small towns and tribes from Amman, its finances and its small Arab Legion underwritten by the British treasury, its borders drawn at the Cairo Conference in a few strokes of the pen.
para4: At the end of 1924 the Hashemite house therefore faced sharply different circumstances in each territory. Ali retained a threatened position in the Hejaz, while Faisal and Abdullah governed in Baghdad and Amman under British influence. The Arab Revolt had not produced the single independent Arab state hoped for by many supporters. The postwar settlement instead joined dynastic ambition, local politics, and European power in several distinct governments whose authority and freedom of action remained contested.

title: The Wahhabi Movement
titleline: The Wahhabi Movement - The History Web
para1: The Wahhabi Movement. The Wahhabi movement (1744-) - its adherents call it the da'wa, 'the call', to pure monotheism - began with one scholar, Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab (1703-1792) of Najd. Preaching a return to the Islam of the first generations, he condemned as idolatry the era's common devotions: pilgrimage to saints' tombs, the veneration of trees and rocks, intercession through the dead, and the mystical excesses of some Sufi orders. Expelled from his home towns, he found in 1744 his protector and partner: Muhammad ibn Saud, emir of Diriyah.
para2: The pact of Diriyah - Saudi sword, Wahhabi creed - powered the First Saudi State's conquests across Arabia, the sack of Karbala (1802), and the occupation and purification of Mecca and Medina (1803-1804), where domes over tombs were demolished - acts that horrified the Ottoman world and provoked Muhammad Ali of Egypt's destruction of Diriyah (1818). The creed survived the state's fall, and returned with the Second Saudi State at Riyadh.
para3: In the twentieth century the compact produced its third state. Abd al-Aziz ibn Saud had retaken Riyadh in 1902 with a handful of men; over two decades he built a new realm on the Ikhwan - settled Bedouin zealots, brought from the desert into agricultural-military colonies and drilled in Wahhabi doctrine - conquering al-Hasa from the Ottomans in 1913, destroying the rival Rashidi emirate of Hail in 1921, and finally turning on the Hashemites: in 1924 the Ikhwan stormed Taif and entered Mecca, driving the sharif's family from the holy city.
para4: By the end of 1924, the capture of Mecca had strengthened Ibn Saud's position, but the struggle for the Hejaz remained unfinished. Ali still held Jeddah, and Saudi control did not yet extend to the whole region. The movement's history through this point shows the importance of the alliance between religious reform and political power. Its growth also provoked resistance and conflict among communities and rulers with different understandings of religious practice and legitimate authority.

title: The Eastern Question
titleline: The Eastern Question - The History Web
para1: The Eastern Question. The Eastern Question (1774-1923) was the century-long diplomatic problem of what should happen as the Ottoman Empire declined: which powers would gain its lands, at what risk of a general European war. It opened with Russia's victory and the Treaty of Kucuk Kaynarca (1774), which gave Russia a protectorate over Ottoman Orthodox Christians - a standing pretext for intervention - and it closed only with the Ottoman Empire's abolition after the First World War.
para2: The 19th century turned on the question repeatedly. Greek independence (1821-1832) created the first nation carved from the empire, backed by Britain, France and Russia. Muhammad Ali of Egypt's invasions (1831-1833, 1839-1841) nearly destroyed the empire from within, saved both times by the European powers. The Crimean War (1853-1856) - Britain and France fighting Russia, ostensibly over the Holy Places - propped the empire up; the Congress of Berlin (1878), after the great Eastern Crisis and Russo-Turkish War, dismembered much of its Balkan territory while Bosnia went to Austria, Cyprus to Britain, and Tunisia (1881) and Egypt (1882) to France and Britain.
para3: For the powers, the question was strategic: Britain guarded the route to India, Russia sought the Straits and Constantinople, Austria feared Slav nationalism, and Germany - building the Berlin-Baghdad railway - replaced them as the empire's patron after 1890. For the Balkan peoples it was the road to nationhood; for the Ottomans, a desperate century of reform (Tanzimat), loans, and maneuver between the vultures.
para4: The question answered itself in catastrophe: the Balkan Wars (1912-1913), the First World War - the Ottoman decision for Germany - and the empire's partition. The Treaty of Lausanne (1923) settled its last terms: the Turkish Republic, the Straits regime, and the mandates. Its afterlife is with us still, in the borders and conflicts of the Balkans and the Middle East.
