title: The Philippine Revolution
titleline: The Philippine Revolution - The History Web
para1: The Philippine Revolution. The Philippine Revolution (1896-1902) was Asia's first anti-colonial national revolution. Spanish rule over the Philippines had lasted three centuries, administered through the friar orders whose abuses - and whose blocking of reform - bred the Filipino ilustrado reform movement of Jose Rizal and Marcelo del Pilar. Rizal's novels Noli Me Tangere and El Filibusterismo indicted the regime; his execution by firing squad in December 1896 turned reform into revolution.
para2: The revolution's instrument was the Katipunan, the secret brotherhood founded by Andres Bonifacio in 1892, whose 'Cry of Pugad Lawin' (August 1896) launched the uprising. Its military genius was Emilio Aguinaldo, who drove the Spanish from Cavite, edged out Bonifacio - executed on Aguinaldo's orders in 1897, the revolution's founding fratricide - and, after a brief truce and exile, returned when the United States destroyed the Spanish fleet in Manila Bay (May 1898). On 12 June 1898 Aguinaldo proclaimed Philippine independence; the Malolos Congress wrote Asia's first republican constitution, and the First Philippine Republic was inaugurated in January 1899.
para3: But Spain had sold the Philippines to America for $20 million at the Treaty of Paris, and the republic's fate was a new colonial war: the Philippine-American War (1899-1902) - conventional battles lost, then guerrilla resistance answered by American 'reconcentration', massacres and water cure at a cost of hundreds of thousands of Filipino lives. Aguinaldo's capture in 1901 and his oath of allegiance broke organized resistance; the last generals surrendered in 1902.
para4: The revolution failed but founded the nation: Rizal its martyr, Bonifacio its plebeian soul, the Malolos Republic its first state. Under American rule the Jones Law of 1916 promised the islands eventual independence, and a generation of Filipino politicians worked the colonial legislature toward it, keeping alive the republic the revolution had founded.

title: The Taiping Rebellion
titleline: The Taiping Rebellion - The History Web
para1: The Taiping Rebellion. The Taiping Rebellion (1850-1864) was the bloodiest war of the 19th century - twenty to thirty million dead - and very nearly destroyed China's Qing dynasty. Its founder, Hong Xiuquan, a failed examination candidate of Guangdong, read Christian tracts and concluded from his fever-visions that he was the younger brother of Jesus Christ, sent to cast down the Qing 'demons' and found the Taiping Tianguo, the 'Heavenly Kingdom of Great Peace'.
para2: From its rising at Jintian (1851), the movement exploded: its God-worshipping converts - disciplined, unqueued, egalitarian in doctrine, communal in property - fought their way north and in 1853 took Nanjing, which Hong made his Heavenly Capital for eleven years. Taiping armies marched to within reach of Tianjin; their proclaimed new order promised land redistribution, equality of women (in principle), and the suppression of opium, footbinding and idolatry - while in practice the Heavenly Kingdom's leaders built palaces and destroyed each other in the horrific Tianjing purge of 1856, when the East King's court slaughtered tens of thousands.
para3: The dynasty, its regular armies useless, was saved by new regional forces: Zeng Guofan's Xiang Army, raised by scholar-gentry to defend Confucian civilization against the Christian heresy, and Li Hongzhang's Huai Army, stiffened by Western-officered units like the 'Ever Victorious Army'. The Qing counterattack strangled the Taiping in the lower Yangzi; Nanjing fell in July 1864, Hong already dead, and the city's sack ended the kingdom.
para4: The Taiping century-shadow is long: it broke the Qing's prestige and shifted power to the regional armies that became warlordism; it devastated China's richest provinces; and Sun Yat-sen, the father of China's republic, grew up on tales of Hong and claimed his revolutionary mantle. Its cost remains the benchmark of civil war's horror in Chinese memory.

title: The Self-Strengthening Movement
titleline: The Self-Strengthening Movement - The History Web
para1: The Self-Strengthening Movement. The Self-Strengthening Movement (1861-1895) was Qing China's first systematic attempt to adopt Western technology to save the imperial system. Born from the double trauma of the Opium Wars and the Taiping Rebellion, it was led by the statesmen who had crushed the Taiping - Zeng Guofan, Li Hongzhang and Zuo Zongtang in the provinces, Prince Gong and Wenxiang at the court's new Foreign Office (the Zongli Yamen, 1861).
para2: The formula, in the scholar Feng Guifen's phrase and Zhang Zhidong's later slogan, was 'Chinese learning as the foundation, Western learning for practical use': Confucian values untouched, Western guns, ships and factories adopted. Over three decades the movement built the Jiangnan Arsenal and the Fuzhou Navy Yard, steamship and telegraph companies, the Kaiping mines and the beginnings of a modern navy - the Beiyang Fleet, by the 1880s nominally Asia's strongest - and sent China's first students abroad and founded interpreters' colleges.
para3: But self-strengthening fought uphill: conservative mandarins saw railways and chimneys as portents; funds were diverted - famously, naval money rebuilt the Empress Dowager Cixi's Summer Palace; the new enterprises were strangled by official corruption and 'official supervision, merchant management'; and the deeper institutions - the examinations, the bureaucracy, the fiscal system - went unreformed, for reforming them was precisely what 'foundation' forbade.
para4: The verdict came in war: Japan, modernized root-and-branch by the Meiji Restoration, destroyed the Beiyang Fleet and took Taiwan in the Sino-Japanese War of 1894-1895. The failure radicalized a generation - toward the Hundred Days' Reform of 1898, then revolution - and left the enduring Chinese debate the movement began: whether technology can be borrowed without the ideas and institutions behind it.

title: The Russo-Japanese War
titleline: The Russo-Japanese War - The History Web
para1: The Russo-Japanese War. The Russo-Japanese War (1904-1905) was the first modern victory of an Asian power over a European empire - and it reshaped the 20th century. Its cause was Manchuria and Korea: both empires' railways, troops and ambitions converged there, and after Russia refused to withdraw from Manchuria as promised and pressed into Korea, Japan - whose diplomacy had failed - struck without declaration, torpedoing the Russian fleet at Port Arthur on 8 February 1904.
para2: The war was fought on a scale the world had not yet seen: the siege of Port Arthur, with its trench lines, machine guns and massed artillery - a preview of 1914 - cost Japan nearly 60,000 men before the fortress surrendered in January 1905. At Mukden (February-March 1905), over half a million men fought the largest battle yet in history to a Japanese victory. Russia's Baltic Fleet, after sailing 18,000 miles around the world, was annihilated in two days at Tsushima (May 1905) by Admiral Togo - losing 21 of 38 ships, one of the most decisive naval victories ever.
para3: Exhausted Japan and revolution-shaken Russia accepted Theodore Roosevelt's mediation: the Treaty of Portsmouth (September 1905) gave Japan Port Arthur, the South Manchurian railway, half of Sakhalin - and a protectorate over Korea, annexed outright in 1910. Tokyo crowds rioted at the 'shameful' peace, which bore no indemnity.
para4: The war's echoes were global: Russia's defeat ignited the 1905 Revolution at home; Japan emerged as the first non-Western great power, its victory electrifying nationalists from India to Egypt and Vietnam; and the Manchurian and Korean prizes fixed the course of Japanese expansion for a generation. Tsushima and Port Arthur remain case studies in every naval and military college.

title: The Nguyen Dynasty
titleline: The Nguyen Dynasty - The History Web
para1: The Nguyen Dynasty. The Nguyen dynasty, founded in 1802, was Vietnam's last imperial house. Its founder, Nguyen Anh - survivor of the Tay Son wars that destroyed the old order - reunified Vietnam in 1802 after a thirty-year struggle, taking the reign name Gia Long and the country's modern name, Vietnam, with his capital at Hue, whose vast citadel-palace, the Imperial City, rose on the Perfume River as a miniature Forbidden City.
para2: Under Gia Long and his son Minh Mang (r. 1820-1841) the dynasty built Vietnam's most centralized Confucian state: a scholar-bureaucracy on the Chinese model, legal codes, land registers, and a claim to suzerainty over Cambodia that brought war with Siam. But the same court persecuted the growing Catholic communities - missionaries and converts executed, churches destroyed - giving France its pretext: French and Spanish forces attacked in 1858, and by 1862-1867 the south (Cochinchina) was a French colony; in 1883-1885, after the Sino-French War, France took the north and center as protectorates, leaving the Nguyen emperors crowned figureheads at Hue.
para3: The dynasty's emperors reigned under French control: the boy-emperor Ham Nghi, who fled his palace to lead the anti-French Can Vuong resistance from the mountains until his capture and exile to Algeria; the young reformist Duy Tan, deposed and exiled in 1916 for conspiring against France; and a line of figureheads crowned and discarded at French convenience. Resistance lived on outside the palace: the reformers of the Dong Kinh Nghia Thuc school taught a modern curriculum in Hanoi in 1907 before the French closed it, and the mandarin Phan Boi Chau sent young Vietnamese to study in Japan and wrote stirring histories of his country's heroes for a new generation of patriots.
para4: Nguyen Vietnam left the country its modern name, its borders, and the monuments of Hue - the Imperial City, the royal tombs along the Perfume River, now UNESCO-listed - while its failure to answer the West set the stage for a century of colonialism, war and revolution.

title: The Modernization of Siam
titleline: The Modernization of Siam - The History Web
para1: The Modernization of Siam. Siam's nineteenth- and early twentieth-century modernization under the Chakri kings Mongkut (Rama IV) and Chulalongkorn (Rama V) made it the only Southeast Asian state never colonized. Mongkut - the scholarly monk-king who had studied English, Latin and astronomy during his 27 years in the monkhood - opened the kingdom deliberately: treaties with Britain (the Bowring Treaty, 1855) and the Western powers fixed low tariffs and extraterritoriality but bought peace, while he hired Western advisers, reformed the calendar and court, and patronized a Buddhist revival.
para2: His son Chulalongkorn (r. 1868-1910) carried reform to the bone: he abolished slavery and the corvee by stages, created ministries, a salaried bureaucracy and a conscript army on Western models, built railways, telegraphs and modern law codes, sent princes to Europe, and centralized the kingdom's outlying tributaries under royal commissioners - while surrendering, with bitter calculation, the periphery to save the core: Laos to France (1893), the Cambodian provinces (1907), the four Malay states to Britain (1909).
para3: The strategy worked: Siam's kings made themselves indispensable to the balance between British Burma and French Indochina, modernized just enough to be treated as civilized, and kept their throne. Bangkok was transformed - Dusit palaces, tramways, the royal temples restored - and a Western-educated elite of princes and commoners staffed the new state.
para4: The price was a contradiction: absolute monarchy had modernized the country, and modernization had created the very classes - officers, officials, Western-educated commoners - who wanted a share of power. Vajiravudh (Rama VI, who became king in 1910) answered with royal nationalism: he founded the paramilitary Wild Tiger Corps to bind the army to the throne, wrote and staged patriotic pageants, brought Siam into the First World War on the Allied side in 1917, and founded Chulalongkorn University in his father's name - but his extravagance and his favorites strained the treasury and alienated the officers the reforms had trained. By 1924 the modernized kingdom faced the questions its own success had raised.

title: The Mutawakkilite Kingdom of Yemen
titleline: The Mutawakkilite Kingdom of Yemen - The History Web
para1: The Mutawakkilite Kingdom of Yemen. The Zaydi imamate of Yemen - one of Islam's longest-lived states - ruled the Yemeni highlands for three centuries, and in its last form, the Mutawakkilite Kingdom, survived into the modern age. The first Qasimi imam, al-Mansur al-Qasim, had raised the Zaydi tribes against the Ottomans in 1597, and his successors expelled them in 1635; thereafter the imams of the Qasim line - chosen, in Zaydi theory, by rising with the sword as learned descendants of the Prophet - ruled from Sanaa and the highland towns, in shifting contest with tribal shaykhs, the coastal powers, and after 1839 the British at Aden.
para2: The Ottomans returned in 1872 and held the coasts and Sanaa for forty years against the imams' stubborn revolts, until Imam Yahya Hamid al-Din fought them to exhaustion and won recognition of his authority by the Treaty of Daan (1911). When the Ottoman Empire collapsed in 1918, Yahya re-established the imamate over all of highland Yemen, ruling from Sanaa as Mutawakkil ('relying on God') - a deliberately sealed kingdom: few roads, no banks, foreign contact minimal, Jewish craftsmen, qat afternoons and medieval governance preserved into the twentieth century.
para3: Imam Yahya ruled his restored kingdom as a fortress. He kept Yemen closed, governing through his sons and the great sayyid families, while disputes multiplied on every border: with Britain over the Aden protectorates, where the frontier was never settled; with the Idrisi ruler of Asir to the north, whose territories he claimed; and with Abd al-Aziz ibn Saud, whose growing power pressed on Yemen from the desert side. The imam claimed authority over all of historic Yemen and recognized no one else's.
para4: By 1924 the Mutawakkilite kingdom stood alone: a Zaydi imamate that had outlasted the Ottomans, armed and unbeaten, but sealed off from the currents reshaping the Arab world around it. Yahya's Yemen was in many ways the state of his Qasimi ancestors preserved - tribal, highland, austere - and its isolation was at once its strength and its danger.

title: The Aceh Sultanate
titleline: The Aceh Sultanate - The History Web
para1: The Aceh Sultanate. The Aceh Sultanate (c. 1496-1903) of northern Sumatra was the greatest Muslim power of the Indonesian archipelago and the fiercest opponent of colonialism in its history. Rising as a pepper port after Malacca's fall, Aceh reached its zenith under Sultan Iskandar Muda (r. 1607-1636), whose fleets and armies dominated both sides of the Straits of Malacca, whose court dazzled foreign envoys, and whose assault on Portuguese Malacca (1629) - 19,000 men, hundreds of ships - failed by a hair.
para2: Aceh's wealth was pepper, and its culture was scholarship: its 17th-century court hosted the great debates of Malay Sufism - the mystics Hamzah Fansuri and Shams al-Din versus the orthodox Nur al-Din al-Raniri - making Aceh 'the verandah of Mecca', the archipelago's gateway to Islam and its premier center of Malay letters. After Iskandar Muda the sultanate declined under four successive queens (1641-1699) and renewed itself in the 19th century as the world's leading pepper exporter.
para3: Its destruction was a generation-long war. When the Dutch, freed by the Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824 and 1871 to act, invaded in 1873, Aceh resisted as no Indonesian state ever had: the sultan died of cholera, but the ulama proclaimed holy war - the Aceh War (1873-1903) - and the Dutch conquered the capital repeatedly while the countryside fought on, at a cost of 100,000 lives and most of the Dutch colonial army's strength, until the last sultan's surrender (1903) and the last guerrilla leaders' defeat by 1912-1914.
para4: Aceh's memory of the war never died. Under Dutch rule the ulama who had led the jihad remained the region's real leaders, the pilgrimage ships carried Acehnese grievances to Mecca and back, and tales of the war were retold in every village and surau. The thirty years' resistance that ended the sultanate had made Aceh's modern identity: a land where Islam, pride and defiance were one - 'the verandah of Mecca', conquered but never quite subdued.

title: The Sultanate of Brunei
titleline: The Sultanate of Brunei - The History Web
para1: The Sultanate of Brunei. The Sultanate of Brunei (1363-) is among the world's oldest continuously reigning monarchies. Islamized under its first Muslim sultan, Muhammad Shah, Brunei rose in the 15th-16th centuries - after the fall of Malacca - into the thalassocracy of Borneo: under the fifth sultan, Bolkiah, its fleets and vassals ranged from Manila and Sulu to Borneo's whole coast, and Magellan's chronicler Pigafetta (1521) marveled at its water-city of 25,000 hearths, the court's elephants and the sultan's gold.
para2: Brunei's long decline began with the Castilian War (1578), when Spain briefly seized and burned the capital, and continued through civil wars and the loss of Sulu and the Borneo coasts. The 19th century brought the fatal amputations: Sarawak was ceded to the British adventurer James Brooke (1841-1842), founding the 'White Rajah' dynasty that ate Brunei's western lands piece by piece; Sabah passed to the British North Borneo Company (1881); and in 1888 the rump sultanate became a British protectorate.
para3: By 1906, when a British Resident took control of the administration, Brunei was nearly gone - its remaining lands split into two enclaves by the loss of the Limbang valley to Sarawak in 1890. The Residency governed in the sultan's name: it reorganized the finances, built roads and a land office, and tidied the succession, while the sultan - from 1918 the young Ahmad Tajuddin - reigned over a protectorate that was a fragment of the empire Bolkiah had ruled.
para4: Yet the protectorate preserved what it diminished. Surrounded by the lands taken by the Brookes and the North Borneo Company, the rump sultanate survived every scheme to partition or absorb it, and the monarchy that had crowned sultans since the fourteenth century passed intact into the twentieth - the oldest reigning house in Southeast Asia, guarded, impoverished, and enduring.

title: The Khanate of Bukhara
titleline: The Khanate of Bukhara - The History Web
para1: The Khanate of Bukhara. The Khanate of Bukhara (1500-1785) was the Uzbek state that inherited Timur's Central Asia. When Muhammad Shaybani Khan, a Chinggisid of the Golden Horde line, swept down from the steppe in 1500, he took Samarkand and Bukhara from the last Timurids and drove the young Babur toward India; his Uzbeks - tribal cavalry organized around oasis cities - made Bukhara their capital and Transoxiana an Uzbek land for four centuries.
para2: Under the early Shaybanids - above all Abdullah Khan II (r. 1583-1598), the last great builder of Uzbek power, who reunified the khanate, campaigned from Khorasan to the steppe, and raised Bukhara's grand architectural ensembles - the khanate controlled the Silk Road's heartland: Samarkand, Bukhara, Tashkent, Balkh and the Ferghana valley. Bukhara became 'the Noble, the Dome of Islam', a city of over a hundred madrasas, where the Naqshbandi Sufi order shaped public life and Persian letters flourished beside Turkic rule.
para3: The 17th-18th centuries under the Janid (Ashtarkhanid) dynasty brought slow decline: the Silk Road trade drained to the sea routes, the khanate fractured against Khiva and Kokand, nomad raids and succession wars multiplied, and the Persian conqueror Nader Shah broke Bukhara's power in 1740, imposing tribute and carrying off its treasures. In the chaos, the Uzbek Manghit clan rose as ataliqs (kingmakers), ruling through puppet khans before taking the throne themselves in 1785 as emirs.
para4: The khanate's legacy is Bukhara itself: its madrasas, the Kalyan complex and the trading domes date overwhelmingly from these centuries, and its world - Uzbek khans, Persian culture, Sunni orthodoxy and Sufi orders - defined Central Asian identity until the Russian conquest.

title: The Al Thani and the Al Khalifa
titleline: The Al Thani and the Al Khalifa - The History Web
para1: The Al Thani and the Al Khalifa. The Al Thani of Qatar and the Al Khalifa of Bahrain - the ruling houses of the two small Gulf states - both descend from the great 18th-century migrations of Arab tribes from Najd to the Gulf coast. The Al Khalifa, leading clans of the Bani Utub confederation, took Bahrain from its Persian garrison in 1783, ruling from Zubarah (on the Qatar coast, now a UNESCO site) before establishing themselves in Bahrain itself; the Al Thani, of the Tamim tribe, emerged as leading pearl merchants and sheikhs of Doha in the mid-19th century.
para2: Both houses rose under the Pax Britannica: Bahrain signed its first treaties with Britain in 1820 and became the Gulf's pearling and commercial hub, seat of Britain's political resident in the Gulf; Qatar's founder-sheikh Jassim bin Muhammad Al Thani asserted independence from both Bahrain and the Ottomans - defeating an Ottoman force at al-Wajbah in 1893 - before accepting an Ottoman garrison and then British protection in 1916.
para3: Both houses ruled maritime societies built on pearls. Each season Bahrain's and Qatar's fleets put out to the oyster banks - thousands of divers bound by debt to the merchants who financed them - and the pearling season fixed the calendar of the whole coast. In Bahrain the Al Khalifa divided the islands' revenues and palm groves among the ruling family, while British agents pressed reforms the notables resisted; in Qatar Sheikh Abdullah bin Jassim, who succeeded his father in 1913, kept a wary balance between the British at sea and the Saudis on his landward border.
para4: By the early 1920s both sheikhdoms stood at the end of the pearling age's long prosperity: Bahrain the Gulf's established port of call, Qatar quieter under its cautious sheikh, each bound by exclusive treaties to Britain, each still ruled by the merchant houses that had won them in the eighteenth century.

title: The Idrisid Emirate of Asir
titleline: The Idrisid Emirate of Asir - The History Web
para1: The Idrisid Emirate of Asir. The Idrisid Emirate of Asir, founded in 1909, was a short-lived theocratic state on the Red Sea coast of southwestern Arabia. Its founder, Muhammad ibn Ali al-Idrisi - a descendant of the Prophet through the Idrisids of Morocco, educated in Fez at the Sanusi order's feet - raised the tribes of Asir in revolt against Ottoman rule from 1909, and by 1911 his fighters held the Tihama coast and its ports, with Italy's quiet support.
para2: In the First World War the emir threw in his lot with Britain: subsidized as an ally of the Arab Revolt, his forces besieged Ottoman garrisons and held the coast, and at the war's end the Idrisid state - recognized by Britain - controlled Asir from the Hejaz border to Yemen, its capital at Sabya. But the emir had two giants for neighbors: Imam Yahya of Yemen to the south and Abd al-Aziz ibn Saud, the rising master of Najd, to the north - and both coveted Asir.
para3: The end came slowly. Al-Idrisi's death in 1920 left his state to minors and feuding uncles, and the emirate's quarrels invited its neighbors in: Imam Yahya of Yemen pressed Asir's southern districts, while Abd al-Aziz ibn Saud, fresh from destroying the Rashidi emirate of Hail in 1921, drew the emir's own family into his orbit. By 1924 the Idrisid state was still standing, and Britain still dealt with it as a government, but its room to maneuver between Sanaa and Riyadh was visibly shrinking.
para4: The Idrisids' experiment mattered beyond its years: it was a revival, in the twentieth century, of the old Arabian imamate tradition - a sayyid of the Prophet's house raising the tribes in his own name - and its fate would help decide where the frontier between Yemen and the rising Saudi power was drawn.

title: The Kurdish Emirates
titleline: The Kurdish Emirates - The History Web
para1: The Kurdish Emirates. The Kurdish emirates (16th-19th centuries) were the semi-independent principalities of Kurdistan, the mountain lands between the Ottoman and Persian empires. When Sultan Selim I defeated the Safavids at Chaldiran (1514), the Kurdish beys chose Ottoman suzerainty - brokered by the scholar-negotiator Idris Bitlisi - in return for hereditary rule: for three centuries, emirates like Bitlis, Hakkari, Bahdinan (Amadiya), Soran, Baban and Bohtan governed themselves, paid tribute and soldiers when it suited them, and warred with each other and the empires on their own account.
para2: The emirates produced a genuine Kurdish high culture. Bitlis under the Sharif khans built its citadel-town and patronized the great Sharafnama (1596), Sharaf Khan Bidlisi's history of the Kurdish dynasties - the first national history of the Kurds. Hakkari and Bahdinan sheltered scholars, dervish orders and the Yezidi communities; the Baban emirs built Sulaymaniyah (1784) into a capital of Kurdish poetry; and the emirs' courts kept Kurdish - in the Hawrami and Kurmanji tongues - a language of letters.
para3: The 19th century destroyed them. Bedr Khan Beg of Bohtan's empire-building - his conquests across Hakkari and the 1843 massacres of the Nestorian Christians - provoked Ottoman intervention (1847) and his exile; the Soran emirate of the 'Blind Emir' Muhammad Pasha of Rawandiz had already been crushed (1836); and the Baban emirate fell in 1850. The Tanzimat state absorbed Kurdistan into directly ruled provinces, leaving leadership to the religious sheikhs - Naqshbandi and Qadiri - whose revolts (1880, and later Barzan and Shaykh Said) replaced the emirs'.
para4: The emirates' memory - self-rule, the Sharafnama's claim to a Kurdish nation, the lost capitals - fed the Kurdish nationalism that emerged precisely from their ruins, and underlies Kurdish politics in Turkey, Iraq, Syria and Iran today.
source3label: Encyclopaedia Iranica: Studies of Modern Kurdish History

title: The Ottomans in Yemen and Arabia
titleline: The Ottomans in Yemen and Arabia - The History Web
para1: The Ottomans in Yemen and Arabia. Ottoman power in southwestern Arabia came in two hard-fought waves. In 1538 Suleiman the Magnificent's admiral Hadim Suleiman Pasha took Aden, and by 1547 the Ottomans held Sanaa and the Yemeni highlands - the empire's southernmost province, prized for the Mocha coffee trade and for closing the Red Sea to the Portuguese. But the Zaydi imams of the highlands, led by al-Mansur al-Qasim and his son al-Mu'ayyad Muhammad, fought a forty-year war that drove the empire out entirely by 1635 - the first great Ottoman retreat of the modern age.
para2: For two centuries Yemen went its own way under the Qasimi imams - the age when Mocha's coffee supplied the world - while Ottoman Arabia contracted to the Hejaz, governed through the sharifs of Mecca and Egyptian garrisons. The Wahhabi wars (1803-1818) then convulsed the peninsula: the Saudis took the holy cities until Muhammad Ali of Egypt, on the sultan's behalf, destroyed Diriyah and occupied the Hejaz and Yemen's coast.
para3: The second Ottoman conquest came in 1849 (coast) and 1872 (Sanaa): the empire built telegraphs, barracks and a vilayet administration, fought the imams' endless revolts - Imam Yahya's uprising from 1904 cost the empire tens of thousands of men and forced the Treaty of Daan (1911), recognizing his autonomy - and held Yemen until 1918, when its garrisons surrendered at the empire's collapse.
para4: The Ottoman centuries left Yemen and Arabia divided along lines that persist: the highland-coast split between Zaydi imamate and Sunni lowlands, the Aden-Hadhramaut separation that became the two Yemens of the 20th century, and a memory of Turkish rule - in the Hejaz, of order and subsidy; in Yemen, of occupation and war - that still colors the region's politics.

title: The Korean Empire and the Protectorate
titleline: The Korean Empire and the Protectorate - The History Web
para1: The Korean Empire and the Protectorate. The Korean Empire (1897-1910) was Joseon Korea's last, doomed attempt to save itself by proclaiming empire. After the Sino-Japanese War (1894-1895) broke China's ancient suzerainty, King Gojong - fleeing Japanese intimidation after the Japanese murder of his queen, Min, in 1895 - took refuge in the Russian legation, then in 1897 proclaimed himself emperor (Gwangmu) of the Great Han Empire, asserting full independence and launching the Gwangmu Reform: modern ministries, a small modern army and navy, tramways and telephones in Seoul, land survey, and the Independence Club's brief flowering of civil society.
para2: Korea's tragedy was geography: it stood at the center of every great power's plans. Russia and Japan contested the peninsula until the Russo-Japanese War settled it - Japan's victory (1905) and the Anglo-Japanese and Taft-Katsura understandings left Korea alone. In November 1905, with troops around the palace, Ito Hirobumi forced the Eulsa Protectorate Treaty on Korea; Gojong's secret appeal to the Hague Peace Conference (1907) was dismissed, and Japan forced his abdication in favor of his feeble son Sunjong.
para3: Resistance was fierce and doomed: the Righteous Armies (uibyeong) - Confucian scholars, soldiers and peasants - fought a nationwide guerrilla war (1905-1910) at terrible cost; Ito himself was assassinated by the Korean patriot An Jung-geun at Harbin (1909). In August 1910 Japan annexed Korea outright, extinguishing a kingdom that had ruled the peninsula since 1392.
para4: The thirteen years of empire are remembered as Korea's missed moment: reform too late, diplomacy outmatched, resistance heroic. The annexation began thirty-five years of colonial rule whose wounds - over collaboration, memory and division - still define both Koreas' relationship with Japan and with each other.

title: The Qing in Inner Asia
titleline: The Qing in Inner Asia - The History Web
para1: The Qing in Inner Asia. The Qing dynasty (1644-1912) was not only a Chinese dynasty but the last great empire of Inner Asia. The Manchus had made themselves masters of the steppe world before ever taking Beijing: allied with the eastern Mongols from the 1630s, ruling through the banner system, the Lifan Yuan (Court of Colonial Affairs), and the emperor's triple identity - Chinese Son of Heaven, Manchu khan of khans, and patron-bodhisattva of Tibetan Buddhism - they built an empire that by 1760 stretched from Korea to the Pamirs and from Siberia to Tibet.
para2: The conquests came in stages. The Qing-Mongol alliance absorbed Inner Mongolia early; the century-long struggle with the Zunghar (Dzungar) Mongols - the last great nomadic empire - ended under the Qianlong emperor with the destruction of Zungharia (1755-1758, its people decimated by war and smallpox) and the conquest of the Tarim Basin (1759), creating 'Xinjiang', the New Frontier, ruled by a military governor and Muslim begs. Tibet came under Qing protectorate after the interventions of 1720 and 1792 (against the Gurkhas); Mongolia was bound by banners, monasteries and debt; and the northeast - the Manchu homeland - was kept as a reserve.
para3: Qing Inner Asia was an empire of deliberate difference: no assimilation, but separate laws, scripts, religions and elites for Mongols, Tibetans, Uyghurs and Manchus, held together by the person of the emperor. Its 18th-century heyday - Qianlong's 'Ten Great Campaigns', the imperial summer capital at Chengde with its Tibetan-style temples - was the largest, most prosperous continental empire on earth.
para4: The 19th century undid it: the great Muslim revolts (Yaqub Beg's Kashgaria, 1864-1877, crushed by Zuo Zongtang), Russian encroachment (Treaty of Beijing, Ili), and after 1911 the fall of the dynasty itself, when Mongolia and Tibet declared independence and the empire's Inner Asian inheritance fragmented - the core of China's modern territorial claims and of Inner Asia's unfinished national questions.

title: The Anglo-Afghan Wars
titleline: The Anglo-Afghan Wars - The History Web
para1: The Anglo-Afghan Wars. Three times between 1839 and 1919 the British Empire marched into Afghanistan, and three times it learned the limits of power in the Hindu Kush. The First Anglo-Afghan War (1839-1842) began as Great Game paranoia: to pre-empt Russian influence, the British deposed Dost Muhammad Khan and installed the exiled Shah Shuja at Kabul with a garrison. The occupation collapsed into catastrophe: an uprising forced retreat, and in January 1842 some 16,000 British and Indian soldiers and camp followers marching out of Kabul were destroyed in the snowbound passes - one surgeon, William Brydon, reaching Jalalabad as the army's symbol.
para2: The Second Anglo-Afghan War (1878-1880) repeated the pattern. Demanding a British mission at Kabul against Russian influence, Britain invaded; its envoy Cavagnari was killed in the Bala Hissar uprising; Kabul was reoccupied and Kandahar besieged, saved at the last moment by Roberts's march (1880) against Ayub Khan. This time Britain settled for control without occupation: it recognized Abdur Rahman Khan, the 'Iron Amir', as ruler, handling his foreign affairs and paying him subsidies - and demarcated the Durand Line (1893), splitting the Pashtun tribes and sowing a border dispute that poisons Afghan-Pakistani relations to this day.
para3: The Third Anglo-Afghan War (1919) was brief and different: the young, reforming King Amanullah attacked British India to assert full independence; a month of frontier fighting and British bombing of Kabul ended with the Treaty of Rawalpindi, which gave Afghanistan control of its foreign affairs - the practical independence the wars had always been about.
para4: The wars' legend - the graveyard of empires - grew from their real lessons: Afghanistan ungovernable by outsiders, the frontier tribes unconquerable, the costs ruinous. Britain's Afghan trauma shaped its strategy for a century, the cautionary tale retold whenever soldiers marched beyond the passes.

title: The Great Game
titleline: The Great Game - The History Web
para1: The Great Game. The Great Game (c. 1813-1907) was the 19th century's longest shadow-war: the rivalry of the British and Russian empires over Central Asia, from the Caucasus to Tibet. Its logic was the map: Russia's armies advanced a generation at a time - into the Kazakh steppe, to Tashkent (1865), Samarkand (1868), Khiva (1873), Kokand (1876) and Merv (1884) - and every Russian mile closer to the Hindu Kush raised British fears for India, the empire's jewel, while London probed north with missions, spies and two invasions of Afghanistan.
para2: The Game was fought mostly by extraordinary men on both sides in disguise and on horseback: the 'pundits' - Indian surveyor-spies like Nain Singh, who measured Lhasa with prayer-wheel and rosary - the officers Burnes, Conolly and Stoddart (the last two executed at Bukhara in 1842), the Russian explorers Przhevalsky and Grombchevsky, and their counterparts, who mapped the Pamirs, dined with khans, and sometimes never came back. Its climaxes were crises: the siege of Herat (1837-38), the Afghan wars, the Penjdeh incident (1885), when Russian and Afghan troops clashed and Europe neared war.
para3: The Game's tools were railways, loans and treaties as much as armies: Russia's Trans-Caspian line, Britain's Indian frontier railways, and finally the Anglo-Russian Convention of 1907, which divided the spoils - Persia into spheres of influence, Afghanistan in Britain's, Tibet neutral - ending the contest as both empires turned to face Germany.
para4: The Game's legacy outlived it: Afghanistan's buffer-state survival, Central Asia's Russian borders, the Durand Line, and a romantic literature - Kipling's Kim gave the Game its name - that made 'Great Game' the permanent shorthand for imperial rivalry in Asia.
source1label: World History Encyclopedia: The Great Game

title: The Anglo-Nepalese War and the Rana Era
titleline: The Anglo-Nepalese War and the Rana Era - The History Web
para1: The Anglo-Nepalese War and the Rana Era. The Anglo-Nepalese War (1814-1816) was fought between the expanding Gurkha kingdom of Prithvi Narayan Shah's heirs and the expanding East India Company, over the Himalayan borderlands. Two years of mountain war - the Gurkhas' kukris against the Company's guns, in forts like Nalapani, where Balbhadra Kunwar's defense became legend on both sides - ended with the Treaty of Sugauli: Nepal ceded a third of its territory (Kumaon, Garhwal, Sikkim's claims) and accepted a British Resident, but was never conquered - the only South Asian state to fight the Company and survive intact.
para2: The war gave both sides a lasting institution: so impressed were the British that they began enlisting the Gurkhas into their own army - the Gurkha regiments that serve Britain and India to this day.
para3: Inside Nepal, the war's aftermath brought a bloody politics of noble factions that ended in the Kot Massacre of 1846: Jung Bahadur Rana butchered his rivals, made himself prime minister, and founded the Rana hereditary premiership, established in 1846 - an extraordinary arrangement in which the Shah kings were kept as ceremonial prisoners in their palace while the Rana prime ministers, office passing brother to brother, ruled as shoguns, building their Italianate palaces (the Singha Durbar), visiting Europe (Jung Bahadur's famous 1850 tour), and keeping Nepal deliberately closed to the world.
para4: The Ranas were loyal allies of Britain - Nepal's troops served in 1857 and in the First World War - and their century preserved Nepal's independence at the price of stagnation and isolation. The Rana palaces still stand in Kathmandu as monuments of the century when a hereditary premiership ruled a sealed kingdom.

title: The Young Turks and the Second Constitutional Era
titleline: The Young Turks and the Second Constitutional Era - The History Web
para1: The Young Turks and the Second Constitutional Era. The Young Turk Revolution of July 1908 - army officers of the Committee of Union and Progress (CUP) forcing Sultan Abdulhamid II to restore the constitution he had suspended in 1878 - was greeted with delirious hope: Greeks, Armenians, Arabs, Jews and Turks embracing in the streets of the empire's cities, parliaments and parties reborn, 'liberty, equality, fraternity' the watchwords of the Second Constitutional Era (1908-1918).
para2: The euphoria died fast. The counter-revolution of April 1909 brought Abdulhamid's deposition, but the CUP - after the Action Army restored order - hardened into power; the Italo-Turkish War (1911) cost Libya, the Balkan Wars (1912-1913) cost nearly all of Europe-in-Turkey, including Salonica, the CUP's home - a trauma that radicalized the triumvirate who seized full power in the January 1913 coup: Enver, the war minister and adventurer; Talaat, the interior minister; and Cemal, the navy minister.
para3: The triumvirs led the empire into the First World War at Germany's side (October 1914), gambling for recovery - and presided over its destruction: the Gallipoli victory and the Kut triumph against Britain, but also the Sarikamish disaster, the Arab Revolt, and the Armenian Genocide (1915-1916), the CUP regime's deportation and massacre of a million Armenians - the defining crime of the era. By 1918 the empire was beaten on every front; the triumvirs fled (all three later assassinated by Armenian avengers), and the Mudros armistice opened the empire's partition.
para4: The Young Turks' decade is the hinge of the modern Middle East: it destroyed the Ottoman ancien regime, pioneered mass politics and party dictatorship, perpetrated genocide - and created, in the ruins, the cadres and the trauma from which Ataturk's Turkish Republic and the Arab successor states alike emerged.
